pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Clear and Active Legal Writing

units.reason: Legal writing now values clarity over ornament.
units.rule: Decide the point first, then phrase it so that most people would understand it on a quick read.

units.reason: Shorter documents are clearer and respect page limits.
units.rule: If an argument can be made in half the pages, make it in half the pages.

units.reason: The active voice identifies both the action and who is responsible for it.
units.rule: Default to actor, verb, object so that each sentence shows who performed the action.

units.reason: The passive is a deliberate tool, not a default.
units.rule: Reserve the passive for cases where the actor is unknown, the statement is a general truth, the thing acted upon deserves the emphasis, or naming the actor would inflame a dispute.

units.reason: Plain words carry the same idea to more readers.
units.rule: Replace Latin and other legalese with ordinary English unless the expression is a true term of art or is needed for the meaning.

units.reason: Doubled words add length without adding meaning.
units.rule: Reduce paired or tripled synonyms to a single word, unless the wording is technical language fixed by a statute or other authority.

units.reason: Noun forms lean on weak verbs and lengthen the sentence.
units.rule: Turn nouns formed from verbs back into verbs, and name who performs the action.

units.reason: Wordy connectors slow the reader and add nothing.
units.rule: When editing, test each word for whether the point needs it, and swap multi-word connecting phrases for one-word equivalents.

units.reason: Single-point sentences are clear, and contrast in length creates emphasis.
units.rule: Keep each sentence to one main point; split longer ones, and use an occasional very short sentence after a long one for force.

units.reason: Counting during drafting gets in the way; the check belongs to revision.
units.rule: Treat about twenty words a sentence as a guide when editing, not a target while drafting.

units.reason: A paragraph carrying two ideas hides the second.
units.rule: Hold each paragraph to one idea, except thesis or concluding paragraphs that briefly gather several.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Memo Writing Checklist

units.failure: a memo that cannot be filed or found
units.reason: Memos are retrieved later by their heading.
units.rule: Complete the heading with recipient, author, date and subject line, and make the subject line useful for filing.

units.reason: A question tied to law and facts tells the reader exactly what is being decided.
units.rule: Frame each question so that yes or no answers it, combining the governing law, the legal issue and the key facts.

units.reason: A question that assumes its answer is no longer a question.
units.rule: Keep the question objective and free of legal conclusions.

units.reason: A busy reader may read only this part and must still get the answer and its basis.
units.rule: Answer each question definitely, then give the reason, the rule and the critical facts in a short passage with few citations.

units.failure: an answer that is conclusory or overloaded
units.reason: Too little gives no basis; too much repeats the discussion.
units.rule: Pitch the short answer between bare assertion and full detail, so that it is clear on a first reading.

units.failure: facts in the order they were learned
units.reason: An ordered account lets the reader form the picture once.
units.rule: Organise the facts logically, by time, by topic, or a mixture of the two.

units.failure: a discussion that relies on unstated facts
units.reason: The analysis must not depend on a fact the reader was never given.
units.rule: Include every legally significant fact, every fact the discussion later relies on, and only as much background as understanding requires.

units.reason: The fact section reports; the discussion evaluates.
units.rule: State the facts neutrally, accurately and briefly, without characterising them or drawing conclusions.

units.reason: The reader sees the whole analysis before entering its parts.
units.rule: Open the discussion with an overview paragraph: the general rule common to every part, any needed background or limits, and a roadmap.

units.reason: A missed element leaves the analysis incomplete.
units.rule: Arrange the discussion so that each element of the statute or cause of action is covered.

units.failure: a prediction the analysis does not support
units.reason: A conclusion at odds with its own reasoning destroys confidence.
units.rule: Begin each issue with a clear prediction, and check that it matches the analysis that follows.

units.reason: Idea-led explanation teaches the rule; a chronology only narrates.
units.rule: Explain a rule by ideas, showing how earlier cases applied it through their facts, reasoning or policy, not case by case in date order.

units.reason: Mixing the two blurs what the law is with how it applies.
units.rule: Keep the client's facts out of the rule explanation; bring them in only when applying the rule.

units.reason: Repeating the facts is not analysis; the link must be made explicit.
units.rule: Mirror the order of the rule explanation when applying it, and spell out how the law connects to the facts.

units.reason: A memo predicts an outcome, so the weak points must be visible.
units.rule: Develop all the relevant arguments objectively, and identify and deal fairly with the counter-arguments.

units.reason: Such openings let the reader follow the logic from paragraph to paragraph.
units.rule: Start each paragraph with a sentence that shows its content and its place in the overall analysis.

units.failure: new argument appearing at the end
units.reason: The ending confirms the analysis; a new idea there is unsupported.
units.rule: In the conclusion, answer the question, sum up the main positions in the order discussed, and add nothing new.

units.failure: unsupported or untraceable statements of law
units.reason: The reader must be able to check each statement of law quickly.
units.rule: Cite wherever support is needed, with pinpoint page references and an explanatory parenthetical where the point is not obvious.

units.reason: A full-thought heading works as an outline of the analysis.
units.rule: Write headings that state a complete thought and show what the text beneath contains.

units.reason: Plain, direct prose in manageable blocks is easier to trust and to follow.
units.rule: Avoid the first person, prefer the active voice, quote sparingly, and keep every paragraph shorter than a page.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Organizing a Legal Discussion: IRAC / CRAC / CREAC

units.reason: A fixed, predictable order stops points being lost or misread.
units.rule: Give every discrete legal issue its own complete unit: issue or conclusion, the governing rule, its application to the facts, and a closing conclusion.

units.failure: several issues tangled in one passage
units.reason: Separating issues keeps one line of reasoning from blurring into another.
units.rule: Put sub-issues under their own subheadings, each with a full unit of analysis.

units.failure: a section that opens with an unanswered question
units.reason: The reader learns the prediction at once and reads the analysis against it.
units.rule: In an objective memo, open each unit by stating the issue together with the likely outcome, not as a bare question.

units.failure: a neutral, tentative opening in a brief
units.reason: Advocacy is stronger when the court knows the position from the first sentence.
units.rule: In persuasive writing, open each unit with the conclusion you are advocating, phrased so that the issue is plain.

units.reason: The reader needs the general rule before its refinements make sense.
units.rule: Shape the rule passage like a funnel: the broadest principle first, then narrower parts and exceptions.

units.reason: Leading with the strongest authority shows what actually controls.
units.rule: Present authorities in order of weight: constitution, statute, regulation, then courts from highest to lowest, and secondary sources only if needed.

units.reason: The reader needs the rule, not a catalogue of decisions.
units.rule: Synthesise one governing rule out of the cases and explain it; do not merely list the cases that apply.

units.reason: Extra case detail hides the rule being drawn from it.
units.rule: Report a case's holding briefly, with only the facts and outcome relevant to your issue.

units.failure: a rule stated with no sense of how it works
units.reason: An illustration makes an abstract rule usable.
units.rule: Where it helps, add a paragraph on a closely relevant precedent, or define a key term, to show how the rule operates in practice.

units.reason: Long quotations bury the words that matter.
units.rule: Trim quoted authority with ellipses and keep block quotations to a minimum.

units.failure: facts and law placed side by side without reasoning
units.reason: Analysis means showing how the law meets these facts, not restating either.
units.rule: Apply the rule to the facts by comparing them with, and distinguishing them from, the authorities already set out.

units.failure: application that drifts from the rule as stated
units.reason: Matching order and wording lets the reader track rule to application.
units.rule: Take the points in the same order as the rule passage and reuse its key terms, even when that means repetition.

units.failure: a unit that ends without an answer
units.reason: The reader should leave each issue knowing the answer.
units.rule: End each unit with one or two sentences giving the conclusion again in concise form.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Introduction to Basic Legal Citation, section 1-100 Introduction

units.reason: Judges may reject an argument that cites nothing, and a lawyer can be sanctioned for it.
units.rule: Give a reference to authority for every statement of law and for every claim about how that law applies.

units.reason: Courts and publishers each use their own variants, so borrowed references come out inconsistent or incomplete.
units.rule: Do not paste a citation from an opinion or another document; check it and put it in the form you need.

units.reason: The manuals are revised every few years, so once-correct forms go out of date.
units.rule: Reformat any citation taken from an older document to match the current standard.

units.reason: These tools leave out exact locations and favour the vendor's own publications.
units.rule: Treat a citation supplied by a research service as raw material: add the pinpoint page or subsection and remove publisher-specific parts.

units.failure: journal-style citations in a practice document
units.reason: The two settings follow different conventions, typography included.
units.rule: For a memo or a brief, use the practitioner form of citation, not the form meant for journals.

units.reason: Some state courts have their own norms, and a federal court in that state may not share them.
units.rule: Find out which citation variant your court expects before you file there.

units.reason: Readers who cite carefully think less of the craft of a writer who does not.
units.rule: Take care over citation form even though it feels like a distraction from the argument.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: legal writing (Wex)

units.failure: a readable but wrong statement of law
units.reason: Legal text is relied on for what the law is, so an error costs more than awkward style.
units.rule: Put accuracy ahead of every other quality, then work for clarity and brevity.

units.failure: explanation pitched at the wrong level
units.reason: The same explanation helps one reader and irritates another.
units.rule: Before deciding what to explain, gauge the reader's needs, degree of interest and legal background.

units.reason: A trained colleague finds them inefficient and annoying.
units.rule: For a lawyer inside your own firm, leave out definitions of elementary legal ideas.

units.failure: a client left unable to follow the advice
units.reason: Without them a simple situation becomes confusing to the lay reader.
units.rule: For a client who has no legal training, explain the basic legal ideas the advice depends on.

units.reason: These documents exist to inform a decision, not to win one.
units.rule: In an office memo or a client letter, weigh the legal problem even-handedly instead of arguing one side.

units.reason: Rudeness or padding provokes hostility in the very person you must convince.
units.rule: Persuade without showing disrespect to the reader, and include only what the reader needs.

units.reason: The forum sets the form and expects filings to match it.
units.rule: When filing with a court or an agency, follow the document style that body prescribes.

units.reason: Court rules usually fix the format for memoranda and briefs.
units.rule: Use the citation format laid down by the rules of the court you are filing in.

units.failure: boilerplate that does not fit the transaction
units.reason: Careless drafting leads to avoidable lawsuits and harms the client.
units.rule: Treat a form or template as a starting point and adapt it to the particular facts of the deal.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: memorandum (Wex)

units.failure: a memo missing a required part
units.reason: These are the parts a legal reader expects to find in a memorandum.
units.rule: Cover five things: the factual background, the legal issues, the governing law, how that law applies here, and a conclusion.

units.failure: a survey of law with no answer
units.reason: A memorandum exists to answer a particular legal question from the sources.
units.rule: Ground the analysis in legal research and organise it so that it supports a conclusion on one defined issue.

units.reason: The court is being asked to accept the argument on the strength of authority.
units.rule: In a persuasive memorandum for a court, show how the governing law and earlier holdings support each argument you make.

units.reason: Lawyers are expected to give a reference for each source they rely on.
units.rule: Cite every legal source the memorandum mentions, in the form the local court rules require.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Drafting a Law Office Memorandum

units.failure: a memo whose parts the reader cannot find
units.reason: This is the conventional layout a legally trained reader looks for.
units.rule: Arrange the memo as heading, question presented, brief answer, facts, discussion, conclusion, in that sequence.

units.failure: a memo that argues instead of predicting
units.reason: The lawyer who asked needs a forecast to act on, not advocacy.
units.rule: Write a forecast of the likely ruling, not a plea to the judge: stay objective and deal with the opposing arguments.

units.failure: a question too broad or stripped of facts
units.reason: A reader should grasp both the legal point and the factual setting at once.
units.rule: Pose one narrow question that joins the legal claim and doctrine to the few facts the answer depends on, and name the jurisdiction.

units.failure: a question that begs its own answer
units.reason: Wording that presupposes the result stops the question from being objective.
units.rule: Keep out of the question any term that already assumes the legal conclusion; save conclusions for the answer.

units.failure: an answer that hedges or needs the discussion to make sense
units.reason: A hurried reader gets the bottom line and its basis without reading on.
units.rule: Open with the direct answer, then give four or five sentences of self-contained reasons applying the rule to your facts, with no citations.

units.failure: an answer that does not match the discussion
units.reason: Thorough readers use it to orient themselves before the detail.
units.rule: Let the short answer mirror the order of the analysis so it doubles as a map of the discussion.

units.reason: The analysis must rest only on facts the reader has already been given.
units.rule: State in the facts section every fact the discussion later relies on, whether it helps or hurts the client, plus background needed for context.

units.reason: A predictive document loses credibility if its facts already advocate.
units.rule: Tell the facts neutrally: no comment, no application of law, no slant toward either side.

units.reason: An evident scheme makes the story easier to follow and to remember.
units.rule: Pick one ordering scheme for the facts — by time, by importance, or by topic — whichever makes them clearest.

units.reason: The reader needs to know where the dispute stands.
units.rule: Name the client and the client's goal, the legal claims in play, and any proceedings that have already happened.

units.failure: a memo that depends on unstated knowledge
units.reason: Several lawyers may consult the memo later, not only the one who assigned it.
units.rule: Recite the facts fully enough that a colleague who knows nothing of the matter could rely on the memo alone, yet keep to what matters.

units.failure: analysis that starts without a map
units.reason: The reader should hold the framework before meeting any detail.
units.rule: Start the discussion with a brief thesis paragraph giving issue, rule and answer, then an introduction that maps what follows and states the whole rule with its parts.

units.reason: This narrows attention to what actually needs analysis.
units.rule: In the introduction, say which points are not in dispute and why, then give the order of the remaining ones.

units.failure: a leap from rule straight to result
units.reason: Skipping a step leaves a gap in reasoning the reader cannot cross.
units.rule: Handle every issue, and every sub-issue, as its own unit: conclusion, rule, explanation of the rule, application, counterargument, conclusion again.

units.failure: a bare rule with no supporting cases
units.reason: The reader may know the area generally but not the decisions you found.
units.rule: After stating a rule, explain it through the cases it comes from, giving their specific facts and reasoning, before you apply it.

units.reason: Prediction depends on comparison with how courts treated similar situations.
units.rule: When applying the rule, set the client's facts beside what the decided cases held and why and show where they match or differ.

units.reason: This shows where the authority is unsettled and tests the main line of analysis.
units.rule: Raise the arguments the other side would likely make and explain why you expect them to fail.

units.reason: The reader judges your credibility by whether your tone fits the state of the authority.
units.rule: Commit to a prediction even when the law is uncertain, and say how confident you are.

units.failure: a question built on the wrong facts
units.reason: Which facts carry legal weight often becomes clear only through writing the analysis.
units.rule: Leave the final wording of the question and the short answer until the discussion is nearly written.

units.failure: an unfamiliar format for the reader
units.reason: Formats vary between offices and the reader's convention governs.
units.rule: Where the office you work for has its own memo format, follow that instead of a textbook layout.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Drafting Briefs to a Court

units.failure: a flat or openly argumentative fact section
units.reason: Judges usually read the facts first, and that reading shapes how they receive the argument.
units.rule: Arrange the facts so they speak to the legal issues and favour your side without arguing openly.

units.failure: argument resting on facts never narrated
units.reason: The fact section and the argument must correspond.
units.rule: Choose facts by the factual tests in the governing statute or case law, and include every fact the argument will use.

units.reason: A narrative holds interest and makes what happened clear.
units.rule: Tell the facts as a story with a plot, people and a viewpoint that a stranger to the case can follow.

units.failure: a story told from the other side's viewpoint
units.reason: Whoever is the grammatical subject becomes the focus of the reader's attention.
units.rule: Make your client the actor at the centre of the story and avoid dwelling on the opponent's experience.

units.reason: A confused reader trusts the client's case less, and the starting point shapes the effect.
units.rule: Keep the sequence of events easy to follow, and choose deliberately where the story starts.

units.failure: a fact section that reads like a pleading
units.reason: A complaint is built to allege each element in numbered paragraphs, not to engage a reader.
units.rule: Do not copy the layout of the complaint when writing the fact section.

units.reason: Omitting them harms accuracy while stressing them harms the client.
units.rule: Give helpful facts the prominent positions, and include damaging facts that matter without dwelling on them.

units.reason: The section persuades through selection and order, not through stated opinion.
units.rule: Strip legal conclusions and editorial comment from the fact section.

units.failure: a brief that starts without orientation
units.reason: The court needs the parties, the posture and the theme before anything else.
units.rule: In the introduction, state your party's claim, introduce your theory through the facts, identify the parties and give the procedural history.

units.reason: The question is the first chance to frame the dispute.
units.rule: Join the claim, the controlling standard and the key facts in one question worded so that the natural answer favours you.

units.reason: A judge reading only the headings should see the whole case and the answer to each question.
units.rule: Write each heading as a legal assertion favourable to your client and tied to facts, so the headings together outline the argument.

units.reason: A fixed pattern lets the court follow each point to its result.
units.rule: Divide the argument into points and subpoints, each running: conclusion, synthesised rule, proof of the rule, application, counterargument, conclusion restated.

units.reason: The relation between neighbouring paragraphs must be evident to the reader.
units.rule: Give each paragraph a single idea; let the next paragraph illustrate it, extend it, contrast with it or move to a related idea.

units.failure: a rule statement cluttered with case facts
units.reason: The detail belongs in the proof that follows.
units.rule: State the synthesised rule in general terms, drawing together the threads shared by several cases, without case detail and framed to favour your side.

units.failure: case summaries with no stated point
units.reason: That opening sentence ties the general rule to its proof.
units.rule: Open each rule-proof paragraph with a sentence carrying one idea from the rule statement, then support it with what the cases held, their key facts and their reasoning.

units.reason: The court will see the difficulty whether or not you address it.
units.rule: Where part of a case cuts against you, distinguish it or explain it instead of leaving it unmentioned.

units.reason: A component left unapplied is a hole in the argument.
units.rule: Apply every component of the legal standard to your facts, and show that the law's underlying policy is served by the result you seek.

units.reason: The reply is needed, yet emphasis on the other side's case strengthens it.
units.rule: Answer the opponent's arguments and dispose of them, but do not give them prominence.

units.failure: paragraphs that do not advance the point
units.reason: If they do not, the organisation of the point is faulty.
units.rule: Test each point by listing its paragraphs' topic sentences in order; they should form a sound outline.

units.reason: Coherence inside and between paragraphs carries the reader forward.
units.rule: Link paragraphs with clear transitions and make each sentence build on the idea of the one before it.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Drafting Client Letters

units.failure: a conclusion buried at the end
units.reason: The client learns at once what was understood and what the answer is.
units.rule: In the first paragraph of an advice letter, restate the client's problem, name the legal question asked and give your conclusion.

units.failure: advice detached from its factual basis
units.reason: If the facts are wrong or change, the client can see that the advice may change too.
units.rule: Set out the legally significant facts as you understand them, and make plain that the advice rests on them.

units.failure: legalese and case names a client cannot use
units.reason: A lay client needs the rule, not the citations.
units.rule: Translate the law into plain language and do not name individual cases.

units.failure: an abstract rule the client cannot picture
units.reason: An illustration lets a non-lawyer see what the rule means in practice.
units.rule: Explain each part of the rule with an example of how it works or of how a court dealt with similar facts.

units.failure: a jump from rule to result
units.reason: The client can follow how the general rule produces the specific answer.
units.rule: Restate your conclusion as you turn to the client's own facts, then apply each part of the rule to them in turn.

units.failure: advice that hides the weak point
units.reason: The client should know the risk as well as the prediction.
units.rule: Mention what the other side could argue and explain why you still hold your conclusion.

units.failure: a legal answer with no practical guidance
units.reason: A client wants to know what to do next, not only who is right.
units.rule: Add practical advice on preventing the same problem in future, weighing non-legal factors such as cost and time.

units.failure: an abrupt ending that closes off questions
units.reason: The letter is one step in a continuing relationship.
units.rule: End by inviting the client to get in touch for a follow-up conversation.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing for understanding | Digital.gov

units.reason: The reader can then see who is responsible for doing what.
units.rule: Make whoever performs the action the grammatical subject of the sentence.

units.reason: That pairing is the usual mark of a passive sentence, which often leaves the doer out.
units.rule: Check sentences for some form of to-be followed by a past participle, and recast them so the actor is named.

units.reason: A writer who confuses them will fix the wrong sentences.
units.rule: Do not mistake a sentence about the past for a passive one; voice and tense are separate things.

units.reason: Forcing an invented actor into such a sentence would be less accurate than the passive.
units.rule: Reserve the passive for rare cases, such as one action following another by operation of law, where there is no actor to name.

units.failure: conditional and future constructions that blur the point
units.reason: Present-tense verbs are the simplest and most direct, so the reader works less to reach the meaning.
units.rule: Write in the present tense as far as possible, including when describing rules or events that began in the past.

units.reason: Sometimes the time relationship is itself part of the meaning.
units.rule: Use another tense only where accuracy needs it, for example when describing what may happen later under stated conditions.

units.reason: Noun forms of verbs lengthen the sentence and drain its force.
units.rule: Keep actions as verbs; when an action has been turned into a noun propped up by a weak extra verb, turn it back.

units.reason: These patterns reliably mark a buried action.
units.rule: Look for nouns built from verbs with typical noun endings, and for such a noun wedged between an article and a preposition, as signs to rewrite.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Clear and short | Digital.gov

units.reason: Small units of information are easier to process, even when the subject is complicated.
units.rule: Give each sentence a single idea, and no more than one.

units.reason: Stacked clauses hide the main point and confuse the reader.
units.rule: Split a sentence heavy with subordinate clauses and exceptions into parts, each part becoming the subject of a sentence of its own.

units.reason: The reader gets shorter sentences without losing the logical relationship.
units.rule: When a condition and its consequence make a sentence too long, put them in two sentences and open each with words that keep the if-then link.

units.reason: Long blocks of text put readers off before they start.
units.rule: Hold most paragraphs to roughly 150 words and between three and eight sentences, and let none pass 250 words.

units.reason: Paragraphs all of one size make the writing feel choppy and dull.
units.rule: Vary paragraph length, and allow an occasional paragraph of a single sentence.

units.reason: Readers can take in one subject at a time and can tell from the first line what a paragraph holds.
units.rule: Confine each paragraph to one topic and open it with a sentence that sums up everything the paragraph contains.

units.reason: Short headed sections look approachable and let readers skim to the part they need.
units.rule: Divide the material into short sections, each under a heading that tells the reader what the section contains.

units.reason: A section that resists a heading is usually covering too much.
units.rule: If a section is too broad to sum up in a meaningful heading, break it into smaller sections.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Style | Digital.gov

units.reason: Readers take an early noun for the main one and have to re-read.
units.rule: Break up runs of three or more nouns: drop the inessential describing words, or add prepositions and articles to show how the words relate.

units.reason: Such phrases pad the sentence without adding meaning.
units.rule: Check phrases built around prepositions; many can be cut down to one or two plain words.

units.reason: Abbreviations send readers back to hunt for the definition; a meaningful short name does not.
units.rule: In place of coining an abbreviation, refer to a long name by a short plain-word name that reminds readers what it is.

units.reason: Explaining the obvious takes up space and irritates the reader.
units.rule: Use an abbreviation without explanation only when it is truly in everyday use; do not define what the reader plainly already knows.

units.reason: Each extra abbreviation is another thing the reader must hold in memory.
units.rule: If an abbreviation cannot be avoided, define it at first use, and keep to two or three abbreviations in one document.

units.reason: Readers follow an argument more easily when each turn is marked.
units.rule: Signal in a paragraph's opening sentence how it relates to the one before: whether it extends, contrasts, or changes direction.

units.reason: These three devices tie new material to what the reader has just read.
units.rule: Link paragraphs by pointing back to something already said, by echoing an earlier idea in new words, or by an explicit connecting word.

units.reason: Writers know their own material and underestimate how much readers rely on these signals.
units.rule: Use explicit connecting words between sentences and paragraphs; neither pile them on nor leave them out because the logic seems obvious to you.

units.reason: A good example can do the work of a long explanation.
units.rule: Clarify a complex idea with an example that fits the reader's own situation; the harder the idea, the more an example is worth.

units.reason: Many readers do not know what the Latin forms mean and mix the two up.
units.rule: Introduce examples and restatements with plain English words; do not use the Latin abbreviations.

units.reason: Positive statements match how people normally think and are understood faster.
units.rule: State what must be done to get the wanted result, not what fails to happen when a condition goes unmet.

units.reason: Two negatives in one clause can reverse the meaning the writer intended.
units.rule: Remove double negatives, including a negative word followed by a word with negative meaning; restate the point positively.

units.reason: A nested exception works like a double negative and is hard to untangle.
units.rule: Rewrite an exception nested inside another exception as a positive statement of the rule.

units.reason: The slash pushes the writer's unresolved choice onto the reader.
units.rule: Do not join alternatives with a slash; decide which you mean, and where both truly apply, spell out that either or both will do.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Scholarly Writing (Goodson Law Library research guide)

units.reason: A paper that repeats published work has no contribution to offer.
units.rule: Before committing to a topic for a legal scholarly paper, survey the existing literature to confirm nobody has already made your argument in the same way.

units.failure: a topic too thin to support a paper
units.reason: A topic with too little material cannot be developed to the needed depth.
units.rule: Use the same early survey to confirm that enough source material exists to sustain a full-length paper.

units.failure: a submission that ignores the journal's rules
units.reason: Journals differ in format and policy, and an unsuitable submission is wasted.
units.rule: Before submitting, read the journal's submission page and some recent issues for its style requirements, and note any exclusive-submission rule.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: 2013 Duke Law Dean's Cup Competition Brief-Writing Guidelines

units.failure: a brief with missing or misplaced parts
units.reason: Courts expect the parts in a set sequence and look for each in its place.
units.rule: Set the brief out in a fixed order under headings: questions presented, the facts, a summary of what is argued, the argument, and a conclusion.

units.failure: a brief that is hard to navigate
units.reason: Judges navigate a brief through its tables.
units.rule: In a full brief, add a table of contents listing argument headings and subheadings with pages, and a table of authorities showing where each is cited.

units.reason: A court can rely only on facts it is able to verify in the record.
units.rule: Confine the fact statement to facts material to the questions under review, each with a reference to the record.

units.failure: a summary that is only a list of headings
units.reason: A real summary lets the court grasp the case before the detail.
units.rule: Write the summary as a clear, accurate condensation of the argument itself, not a repeat of the argument headings.

units.reason: An assertion without reasons and support does not persuade a court.
units.rule: For each contention give the reasons behind it, citing the authorities and the parts of the record relied on.

units.failure: an argument with no standard of review
units.reason: The standard tells the court how closely to examine the decision below.
units.rule: Give the review standard that applies in a concise statement, either inside the treatment of each issue or beneath its own heading placed ahead of it.

units.reason: The court must know precisely what it is being asked to do.
units.rule: Keep the conclusion short and name the exact relief the party asks the court to grant.

units.reason: Breaking the formal limits is penalised whatever the quality of the argument.
units.rule: Keep within the stated page or word limit and the prescribed typeface and margins.

units.reason: Briefs are judged in part on how well they handle the other side's best points.
units.rule: Keep to the legal issue that matters and confront the arguments and authorities that cut against your position.

units.reason: Organisation and style carry as much weight with scorers as legal analysis.
units.rule: Order the argument logically and write in a consistent, persuasive style that shows conviction in the position.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Literature review

units.reason: Evaluation is what separates reviewing the literature from merely reporting it.
units.rule: Do two things in a literature review: cover what studies, theory and evidence already exist, then evaluate and discuss that material critically yourself.

units.reason: The review has to demonstrate grasp of the field, not only acquaintance with individual texts.
units.rule: Place the literature on your specific topic in its wider context, showing both knowledge and understanding of it.

units.reason: Showing the contested areas proves real familiarity with the state of the debate.
units.rule: Summarise and analyse earlier research and theory, and point out where claims are disputed.

units.failure: no gap established for the new study
units.reason: Knowing what is missing is what frames and justifies new research questions.
units.rule: Bring out the gaps in research to date, so that it is clear what remains unknown within the topic.

units.reason: A review that only accumulates sources makes no case.
units.rule: Select and arrange sources so they make an argument; do not simply display everything collected.

units.failure: unrevised review with a broken line of argument
units.reason: A review, like any writing, reaches a clear line only through revision.
units.rule: Rework and re-edit parts of the review, stepping back to check the overall structure and whether the argument flows.

units.reason: Good academic practice requires credit for all material drawn on.
units.rule: Acknowledge the work of others throughout the review by citing and referencing every source.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Academic writing

units.failure: answering a different question from the one set
units.reason: A response is judged by whether it does what the task directs.
units.rule: Before writing, study the directive terms of the brief or title, since they state what you are required to do.

units.failure: evidence laid out without an argument
units.reason: Evidence without a position is not an argument.
units.rule: Do not stop at presenting good evidence; use it as reasons supporting a point of view the reader can be persuaded of.

units.failure: no argument until the final paragraph
units.reason: A working answer gives direction to reading and lets the argument grow with the draft.
units.rule: Form a provisional answer to the brief early and keep refining it while reading and drafting.

units.failure: material left in the order it was read
units.reason: Notes arrive as fragments, and the persuasive sequence has to be discovered.
units.rule: Try different orderings of your notes and material until the sequence of reasons becomes persuasive to a reader.

units.failure: ideas run together in undivided text
units.reason: Paragraph breaks show the reader where one idea ends and the next begins.
units.rule: Treat each paragraph as a unit that organises one piece of your thinking, and consider deliberately when to start a new one.

units.failure: workplace-style lists in place of argument
units.reason: Academic writing is about developing an argument, which lists cannot carry.
units.rule: In academic work, write concise connected prose and do not present the content as bullet points.

units.reason: Academic readers accept claims on the strength of evidence and scholarship.
units.rule: Ground statements in appropriate, informed sources and do not rest them only on personal opinion or experience.

units.reason: Careful wording matches the strength of a claim to its evidence.
units.rule: Make few absolute statements; phrase claims in suitably tentative or cautious language.

units.failure: applying one subject's conventions to another
units.reason: What counts as correct form depends on the discipline and the type of document.
units.rule: Check course guidance and the brief for the expected purpose, format and structure, because conventions differ between subjects and kinds of task.

units.reason: Good structure and expression usually emerge through revision.
units.rule: Treat writing as a cycle of planning, drafting and reviewing, expecting to change the plan and redraft some sections.

units.reason: Markers expect to see whose thinking each idea is.
units.rule: Attribute accurately every idea taken from others, including ideas from those who teach you.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Regulatory Drafting Guide: Avoiding Ambiguity

units.reason: Word position is the chief signal of how words relate.
units.rule: Place each modifier beside the words it qualifies, and keep related words together.

units.failure: a pronoun with two possible referents
units.reason: A reader cannot ask which one was meant.
units.rule: Repeat the noun whenever a pronoun could point to either of two people or things.

units.reason: The grouping allows more than one reading of the sentence.
units.rule: Do not string several prepositional phrases together where it is unclear what each attaches to.

units.reason: Otherwise the start and end are open to dispute.
units.rule: Fix a time period by stating its first and last days, and say "day" when the period is counted in whole days.

units.failure: provisions frozen or floating by accident
units.reason: Readers cannot tell if the provision tracks later changes in that fact.
units.rule: Leave out words tied to the drafting moment; write the specific fact in, or say expressly that it changes over time.

units.reason: A phrase such as "more than" an age can mean either of two birthdays.
units.rule: State an age limit exactly, by naming the birthday or age at which it begins.

units.reason: Provisos are archaic and produce long sentences that are hard to understand.
units.rule: Replace a proviso with a plain connective for a limit, an exception or a condition, or start a new sentence.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Regulatory Drafting Guide: Principles of Clear Writing

units.reason: "Shall" can be read either as an obligation or as a forecast.
units.rule: Impose a duty with "must", grant discretion with "may", predict with "will", and do not use "shall".

units.reason: A rule speaks at the moment it is applied, not when it was written.
units.rule: Write the provisions of a regulation in the present tense throughout.

units.reason: Each added negative makes the reader work out what is actually allowed.
units.rule: Express an idea positively where that is accurate, keep a negative for a warning, and never stack several negatives.

units.failure: a rule defined only by what it excludes
units.reason: Readers need the category before they can make sense of what falls outside it.
units.rule: State a rule or class directly instead of through its exceptions; if an exception is shorter, give the rule first and the exception second.

units.reason: A plural leaves open whether the rule applies to each member or to the group jointly.
units.rule: Use the singular noun wherever the meaning allows.

units.reason: In a rule a change of term is read as a change of meaning.
units.rule: Keep to one word for one thing throughout, and never reuse that word for a different thing.

units.failure: a list mixing phrases, clauses and topics
units.reason: Matching form shows the items are of the same kind.
units.rule: Give parallel ideas the same grammatical form, especially the items of a list.

units.reason: Verb-based sentences run shorter and read as more direct.
units.rule: Use the action verb in place of the noun built from it.

units.reason: The imperative avoids the passive and yields shorter, crisper steps.
units.rule: Give procedures and lists of duties as direct commands.

units.reason: Plain strong wording is dignified without being pompous.
units.rule: Choose the simple word, cut compound prepositions, and drop one of any two words that mean the same.

units.reason: A noun string can be read in more than one way.
units.rule: Break up a stack of nouns by adding prepositions that show how the words relate.

units.failure: gendered wording, or a meaning shifted in revision
units.reason: Switching to a plural, for instance, can change who must do what.
units.rule: Avoid gendered terms, and check that the rewrite has not altered the meaning.

units.reason: The more clauses, the more room for doubt about intended meaning.
units.rule: Limit each sentence to a single point, and divide a long sentence into two or three.

units.reason: Position decides whether the reader meets the point before losing track.
units.rule: Put a simple condition or two ahead of the rule; put multiple complex conditions after the rule; turn several conditions into a list.

units.failure: list items that do not connect to the introduction
units.reason: The reader should be able to read any single item with the introduction and get a whole statement.
units.rule: Word each list item so that, joined to the lead-in, it makes a whole statement.

units.reason: Compact, unified paragraphs are easier to follow.
units.rule: Keep paragraphs short and on one topic; spread a long technical discussion across several linked paragraphs.

units.reason: Abstract wording is vague and open to differing interpretations.
units.rule: Phrase an instruction in plain, concrete terms and avoid abstract ones.

units.failure: a hostile tone toward the regulated reader
units.reason: Word choice can win a reader's cooperation or provoke resentment.
units.rule: Avoid words likely to antagonise the people who must comply.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Making Regulations Readable

units.reason: Section headings appear in the contents, which readers use as their map.
units.rule: Plan a regulation through its table of contents, and put the key topics into section headings instead of burying them in paragraphs.

units.reason: Each kind of reader can go straight to the part meant for them.
units.rule: Gather any long sequence of sections (about ten upward) under parts arranged by function, by stage of the process or by type of reader.

units.reason: The order should follow the reader's needs, not the drafter's history.
units.rule: Sequence sections by what readers need first: major before minor, usual before rare, first step before last.

units.reason: A vague heading forces the reader to study the text to learn whether it applies.
units.rule: Write longer, informative headings, often phrased as questions, in place of a vague one- or two-word label.

units.reason: Similar-sounding headings send readers to the wrong place.
units.rule: Check that neighbouring headings can be told apart and that the sections leave no gaps, overlaps or contradictions.

units.failure: long sections with nothing to navigate by
units.reason: Few people read a regulation straight through; most jump to what concerns them.
units.rule: Use many short sections, each with a heading.

units.reason: Deep nesting is hard to follow and to cite.
units.rule: Keep paragraph nesting shallow: seldom three designated levels and never more; make additional sections instead.

units.failure: multi-branch rules packed into a sentence
units.reason: Side-by-side layout shows relationships that prose obscures.
units.rule: Set out complex options, conditions or steps in an if-then table, and sketch a flow chart to test how the parts fit.

units.reason: Direct address turns a vague statement of fact into an instruction with an owner.
units.rule: Address whoever must comply as "you", and establish who that is by a definition, a heading or an opening clause.

units.reason: Only one person reads at a time, and a newcomer needs things spelled out.
units.rule: Write to a single reader, and assume that reader is new to the regulation.

units.reason: A passive seldom says who or what performs the action.
units.rule: Allow only a handful of passive verbs on each page, and repair them by placing the doer ahead of the verb or by changing the verb.

units.reason: A sentence should be clear on a single reading.
units.rule: Aim for an average near fifteen words a sentence, and go past thirty only when the sentence finishes with a parallel list.

units.failure: a main clause delayed by conditions
units.reason: Otherwise the reader must hold everything in mind before learning the point.
units.rule: When a sentence carries several complicated qualifications, lead with its main clause and let the qualifications follow.

units.failure: interrupting phrases in the middle of the core
units.reason: An interruption there makes the reader wait for the meaning.
units.rule: Keep a subject next to its verb, and keep the parts of a compound verb together.

units.reason: Patch upon patch leaves a structure that no longer serves anyone.
units.rule: After many piecemeal amendments, redraft from a blank page with the reader's convenience in mind.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: White Papers | The Writing Center, George Mason University

units.failure: a paper with no clear line from problem to answer
units.reason: Readers come to learn about a problem and what can be done about it, in that order.
units.rule: Build the paper on a problem-then-solution frame: summary, background, the problem, one or more solutions, then a conclusion.

units.failure: a sales pitch dressed up as analysis
units.reason: Decision-makers must trust that the writer has weighed the whole picture from their side.
units.rule: Keep the tone objective and informative, not persuasive, even where the paper recommends one course of action.

units.reason: Leaders use the paper to inform decisions, so it has to be both readable and well grounded.
units.rule: Write for decision-makers and interested citizens who want detailed knowledge of the problem: accessible in style, with authoritative sources as evidence.

units.failure: a summary that does not match the paper
units.reason: It can only reflect the paper accurately once the paper exists.
units.rule: Draft the executive summary last; in brief it covers the problem, the solutions offered, and any recommendation.

units.reason: Readers need the setting before they can judge the problem.
units.rule: Use the introduction or background to set the context: relevant history and whatever actors, laws or technologies shape the policy situation.

units.failure: a problem asserted but never analysed
units.reason: A problem is only fully stated when its cause and consequences are visible.
units.rule: Cover three elements of the problem: the situation to be changed, what causes it, and the harm that results; consider signposting each.

units.reason: The genre rests on careful research and cited facts.
units.rule: Back with evidence every fact that shows the problem exists, what causes it and what harm it does.

units.reason: Separate sub-sections keep a many-sided problem from becoming a tangle.
units.rule: When the problem is complex, give each aspect of it a sub-section of its own.

units.failure: solutions that do not address the cause
units.reason: A plan that does not act on the stated cause will not be accepted as a real answer.
units.rule: Frame the root cause with care, because it determines which solutions will look logical.

units.failure: time spent on options that could never qualify
units.reason: Stated criteria rule out whole classes of options that then need no discussion.
units.rule: Where it helps, state the criteria any acceptable solution must meet before presenting solutions.

units.reason: Readers cannot weigh an option that is only sketched.
units.rule: Set out each solution in detail, with sound evidence for the information given.

units.failure: a mismatch between problem and solution
units.reason: Alignment between problem and answer is what makes the paper credible.
units.rule: Check that every solution follows logically from the way the problem and its cause were described.

units.reason: Readers deciding between options need to see what each does well and badly.
units.rule: What current solutions do well and badly may be assessed inside the solution section or in a separate evaluation section.

units.reason: A recommendation persuades only when it is shown to be practical and effective.
units.rule: If recommending, set out the proposed course of action in light of the options and how each fares, with evidence that it is feasible and will work.

units.reason: The ending is the reader's last reminder of what matters.
units.rule: Close by restating the paper's most important points, or by restating why the problem needs to be dealt with.

units.reason: Meticulous sourcing is part of what gives the genre its authority.
units.rule: Finish with a list of every source cited, headed as the citation style in use requires.

units.reason: Specific wording tells readers what this paper, and each part of it, is about.
units.rule: Give the paper a descriptive title, and replace generic section labels with headings specific to the issue discussed.

units.reason: The two share a form but differ in audience, purpose and typical length.
units.rule: Know which kind you are writing: a policy paper examines a problem and its options, while a business one presents a product or service as the solution.

units.failure: padding or cutting to an arbitrary length
units.reason: Depth should follow what the issue requires, not a fixed template.
units.rule: Let how complex the issue is set the length of a policy paper, from a few pages to several dozen; visuals are optional.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Checklist for the Memorandum

units.reason: The reader relies on the memo to make a decision and needs a neutral assessment.
units.rule: Write to inform, not to argue: explain the law, weigh both the strong and the weak points, and predict how the question will come out on these facts.

units.failure: memo that wanders beyond its question
units.reason: Material outside those limits does not help the reader with the decision at hand.
units.rule: Stay inside the question asked, the governing jurisdiction and the limits of the assignment.

units.reason: Legal readers expect this layout and know where to look for each thing.
units.rule: Use the customary parts in order: heading block, question presented, brief answer, facts, discussion, conclusion; drop a part only when the reader does not need it.

units.reason: These details identify the document and its context at a glance.
units.rule: Label the document as a memorandum and give recipient, author, date and subject at the top.

units.reason: A complete question lets the reader grasp the issue without reading further.
units.rule: Frame the question neutrally, naming the applicable law or jurisdiction, the precise legal issue and the facts that matter most legally.

units.reason: An overlong question is hard to take in.
units.rule: Shorten the question if it runs beyond a few lines or cannot be read aloud in a single breath.

units.failure: answer that hedges or merely restates the question
units.reason: The reader wants the bottom line and its reason before the full analysis.
units.rule: Answer the question directly and concisely, adding a short statement of the legal basis and the facts the outcome turns on, leaving out formal cites and quoted passages.

units.failure: analysis relying on facts never stated
units.reason: The analysis must rest on facts the reader has already been given.
units.rule: Tell the legally significant facts completely and neutrally, and make sure every fact used later in the analysis appears here.

units.reason: Unused facts either signal a gap in the analysis or are clutter.
units.rule: For each stated fact the analysis never uses, decide whether it is needed background, belongs in the analysis, or should be cut.

units.reason: Conclusions presented as facts prejudge the analysis and undermine objectivity.
units.rule: Keep legal conclusions out of the fact section.

units.failure: roadmap and body out of step
units.reason: A preview that the text honours lets the reader track the analysis.
units.rule: Open the discussion with a roadmap, and then follow in the large-scale organization exactly the order the roadmap announced.

units.reason: A repeated pattern makes the reasoning predictable and easy to check.
units.rule: Treat each element, factor or sub-issue separately, applying the same analytical pattern to each one.

units.reason: How the rule is structured determines how it must be applied.
units.rule: State the governing test and its type: whether all elements are required or one suffices, how factors rank, or which interests a court weighs and how heavily.

units.failure: case summaries with no synthesis or application
units.reason: A prediction is only as sound as the rule and application behind it.
units.rule: Combine the authorities into a synthesized rule, apply it to the facts with reasoning, and cite all binding authority.

units.reason: The reader needs both the likely result and the risks.
units.rule: Address counterarguments fairly and still commit to a prediction or recommendation while admitting its weak points.

units.reason: Framing each stage tells the reader what is coming and what was established.
units.rule: Start each stage of the analysis with a short introduction and finish it with a short conclusion.

units.reason: Topic sentences guide skimming readers and very long paragraphs hide the point.
units.rule: Let topic sentences lead the reader from point to point, and break up any paragraph that fills most of a page.

units.reason: Plain, measured prose serves a reader who must act on the analysis.
units.rule: Keep the tone neutral, vary sentence length, avoid tangled constructions and needless legal jargon, and explain terms of art while using them precisely.

units.reason: The two sections share a job, so one may be short where the other is thorough.
units.rule: Summarize the findings at the end, choosing its length deliberately in light of how full the brief answer already is.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Tips for Achieving Clarity in Contract Drafting

units.reason: A contract governs future conduct and is written down to head off later disputes.
units.rule: Draft every sentence so that it can be read in only one way, the way you intend.

units.reason: Drafting without knowing the client's needs produces terms that do not fit the deal.
units.rule: Before drafting, outline the provisions needed and the client's position and appetite for risk on each.

units.reason: A model saves effort but may be incomplete, foreign or outdated.
units.rule: Start from earlier agreements as models, comparing several, and check each for the needed provisions, its governing jurisdiction and whether the law has changed since.

units.reason: The parties and any judge who later interprets the contract must be able to read it easily.
units.rule: Replace archaic legal wording with plain English that every party can follow.

units.reason: Shorter sentences are easier to read and to interpret.
units.rule: Rework any sentence longer than about three lines, either by splitting it or by setting its parts out as sub-sections.

units.reason: Readers skim past dense blocks, and a heading that misdescribes its content misleads.
units.rule: Divide large provisions into sections and sub-sections with headings, and make sure each heading accurately describes everything beneath it.

units.reason: In a contract a different word invites the reading that a different thing is meant.
units.rule: Use one term for one thing throughout; never vary wording for the sake of style.

units.failure: unused or inconsistently used defined terms
units.reason: Stray or misused definitions create doubt about meaning.
units.rule: Check that each defined term is used exactly as defined and capitalized every time, and delete definitions that are never used.

units.reason: References carried over from another document often point to the wrong place.
units.rule: Verify every cross-reference, especially after adapting a model agreement, so that it points to the right section of this contract.

units.failure: obligation verb with no party as its subject
units.reason: Keeping the two apart shows which statements impose duties.
units.rule: Reserve the verb of obligation for a duty placed on a named party, and use the simple future for consequences that bind no one.

units.reason: Courts normally read that verb as optional.
units.rule: Use the permissive verb only to grant a party discretion to act, not to impose a duty.

units.reason: Contracts oblige parties to act, so the actor and the act should be plain and unbroken.
units.rule: Prefer active constructions, keeping subject, verb and object next to one another, moving qualifying phrases to the end.

units.reason: A noun in place of a verb hides who is responsible for acting.
units.rule: Express actions as verbs with a named actor instead of as abstract nouns.

units.reason: Readers cannot otherwise tell whether it applies to all items or only the nearest.
units.rule: Where a qualifying phrase sits beside a series or compound, make clear which items it governs, using commas if needed.

units.reason: The same word qualifying different parts of a sentence sets a higher or lower threshold.
units.rule: Place a materiality qualifier deliberately, since where it sits changes how demanding the obligation is.

units.reason: Gendered wording can mislead, distract or offend readers.
units.rule: Avoid gendered pronouns: make the noun plural, or repeat the noun itself.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing Effective Point Headings

units.reason: Headings both organize the argument and persuade.
units.rule: Write each heading in the argument as a full sentence that states a conclusion on a legal issue, not as a topic label or a question.

units.failure: headings that do not add up to an argument
units.reason: A busy judge may read nothing else.
units.rule: Test the headings by reading them alone on the contents page; together they should give a complete and convincing outline of the case.

units.failure: two grounds merged in one heading
units.reason: Separate grounds stand or fall separately and should be seen that way.
units.rule: Give each independent ground for relief its own major heading, matching the issues before the court, and order them logically, for instance strongest first.

units.reason: Subdivision lets each reason be analysed in turn.
units.rule: Add lower-level headings when a major point needs several supporting arguments, such as each element or factor of the test.

units.reason: A division into one part is no division.
units.rule: Never leave a lone sub-heading under a heading; fold a single sub-point into the heading above.

units.failure: reader lost in a long section; repetitive sections
units.reason: Heading depth should match the complexity the reader must follow.
units.rule: Subdivide further when an argument runs many paragraphs or rests on several criteria, and merge sub-headings whose subject matter overlaps.

units.reason: Visual distinction shows the hierarchy, and local rules may dictate form.
units.rule: Follow the court's and the practice area's format rules for headings, and style each heading level differently.

units.reason: Previews tell the reader how the sections fit together.
units.rule: Begin the argument with a roadmap of the issues and give each major section a shorter one of its own.

units.reason: The reader needs conclusion and reason together, but one heading cannot carry everything.
units.rule: In a heading with no subdivisions, include the rule, your conclusion and the key facts and reasoning; where sub-headings follow, let the main heading state the conclusion and the sub-headings supply facts and reasons.

units.reason: Positive statements convince more readily, and commanding a court is improper.
units.rule: Phrase headings affirmatively where possible, and do not word them as orders to the court.

units.reason: Precise facts persuade where exaggeration weakens credibility.
units.rule: Make headings memorable through exact facts and strong wording, leaving out adjectives and adverbs that only inflate the claim.

units.reason: Early headings expose gaps and repetition, but they must grow with the draft.
units.rule: Draft the headings first as an outline of the argument, then revise them as the argument develops, working in the key facts and reasoning.

units.reason: Dropping it keeps headings concise.
units.rule: Leave the request for relief to the conclusion instead of repeating it in every heading.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Technical Writing One: Documents

units.failure: reader hunting for content that is not there
units.reason: Stating limits sets expectations and gives the writer a test for what belongs.
units.rule: Begin by saying what the document covers, and also name the related subjects a reader might expect that it leaves out.

units.reason: A document and its declared scope must agree.
units.rule: Use the scope statement as a check while drafting: if content strays from it, either cut the content or rewrite the scope.

units.reason: Irrelevant exclusions add noise and confuse.
units.rule: List as out of scope only subjects a sensible reader could expect; do not mention things nobody would look for here.

units.failure: wrong reader struggling through unsuitable material
units.reason: Readers can then tell at once whether it suits them and what to prepare.
units.rule: Say who the document is for, and state any knowledge, experience or earlier reading it takes for granted.

units.failure: key point buried deep in the text
units.reason: Busy readers seldom finish long documents.
units.rule: Put the essential answers at the very start, on the assumption that many readers will stop after the first paragraph.

units.reason: The start carries the most weight with readers.
units.rule: Expect to rewrite the opening page several times; it is the hardest part and decides whether anyone reads further.

units.failure: new concept presented in a vacuum
units.reason: Most work extends existing ideas, so a familiar reference point speeds understanding.
units.rule: Explain a new idea by setting it beside something the audience already knows, noting what is alike and what differs.

units.reason: A minor detail there displaces what readers were promised.
units.rule: Keep the first paragraph to the most important matters and follow through on whatever it leads readers to expect.

units.failure: content chosen without regard to the reader
units.reason: These answers decide what the document must contain.
units.rule: Before outlining, settle four things: who the readers are, why they are reading, what they know already, and what they should know or do afterwards.

units.failure: structure that mirrors the writer's process
units.reason: Organization should follow reader needs, not the order the writer thought of things.
units.rule: Build the outline from the readers' goals so each section delivers something they came for, in an order that serves them.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Technical Writing One: Lists and tables

units.reason: The list type itself tells the reader whether sequence counts.
units.rule: Number a list when the order of its items matters and use bullets when the items could be shuffled without changing the meaning.

units.reason: Items crammed into running prose are hard to scan in technical material.
units.rule: Pull a series of items packed inside a sentence out into a bulleted or numbered list.

units.reason: The first item sets a pattern readers expect the rest to follow.
units.rule: Make every item in a list match the others in grammatical form, kind of thing, capitalization and punctuation.

units.failure: steps that describe instead of instruct
units.reason: A command at the front tells the reader immediately what to do.
units.rule: Start each numbered step with a command verb, and keep all steps in that same form.

units.reason: Consistent mechanics keep lists tidy and predictable.
units.rule: Capitalize the first word of each list item and end an item with sentence punctuation only when it is a full sentence.

units.reason: Readers should never have to guess what a column means.
units.rule: Give every table column a heading that says plainly what the column holds.

units.reason: Tables are for quick comparison and long text defeats that.
units.rule: Keep table cells short; if a cell needs more than a couple of sentences, present that content some other way.

units.failure: mixed data types in a column
units.reason: Readers scan down a column and expect like to sit with like.
units.rule: Keep the entries within one column of the same kind, even though separate columns may hold different kinds of data.

units.failure: list or table with no introduction
units.reason: The lead-in supplies the context a bare list or table lacks.
units.rule: Precede each list or table with a sentence saying what it shows, and end that sentence with a colon.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Technical Writing One: Paragraphs

units.failure: opening sentence that points at the wrong subject
units.reason: Hurried readers often read only first sentences and skip the rest.
units.rule: Make the first sentence of each paragraph state that paragraph's main point, and spend the most effort on it.

units.reason: A paragraph works as a single unit of reasoning, and stray sentences blur it.
units.rule: Hold each paragraph to one topic; when revising, cut or relocate any sentence that does not bear directly on it.

units.reason: Large blocks of text look forbidding and readers pass over them.
units.rule: Aim for paragraphs of about three to five sentences and split those that run past roughly seven.

units.reason: A run of one-sentence paragraphs is a sign that the material has not been organized.
units.rule: Where a document has many single-sentence paragraphs, merge them into fuller paragraphs or turn them into a list.

units.failure: statement with no stated importance or use
units.reason: A point without relevance or application leaves the reader unable to act on it.
units.rule: Check that a paragraph tells the reader what the point is, why it matters to them, and how to use it or how they can know it holds.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: A guide to technical report writing

units.failure: report that covers the wrong ground or tries to be two documents
units.reason: Without fixed aims the report is harder to write, harder to follow and less likely to get the response wanted.
units.rule: Before writing, note down who the report is for, why it is being produced and what it will cover, and keep checking against those notes to the end.

units.failure: content pitched at the wrong level
units.reason: Reader knowledge and the response sought should set the approach, the technical depth and the style.
units.rule: Work out what the reader already knows, what they must be told and what you want them to do, then write to close that gap.

units.failure: main text cluttered with marginal material
units.reason: Sorting by relevance keeps the body short and focused.
units.rule: Sort gathered material three ways: relevant to the aims (main text), possibly useful to some readers (appendix), and merely interesting to you (set aside).

units.reason: A lean main text stays readable while specialists can still find the detail.
units.rule: Move into appendices whatever most readers do not need, such as detailed data, glossaries or costings.

units.failure: patronised experts or confused lay readers
units.reason: Experts dislike over-explanation and non-experts need it; appendices satisfy both.
units.rule: Use appendices to serve mixed audiences in one report, placing extra explanation or specialist detail where only those who want it will look.

units.reason: Specific headings add white space and let readers go straight to the parts that concern them.
units.rule: Divide the content beneath headings, each worded as precisely as its content permits.

units.reason: A familiar frame helps readers find things, and it can be adjusted to fit.
units.rule: Absent a house template, use the usual frame: title page, summary, contents, introduction or scope, procedure, findings, conclusions, recommendations, references, appendices; merge or adapt as the reader needs.

units.reason: A common numbering scheme shows how sections relate, and deep nesting is hard to follow.
units.rule: Number headings decimally so that the numbering depth shows rank, with no more than four levels; mark appendices with letters.

units.reason: Accurate references make the report more believable, and details noted late are where mistakes arise.
units.rule: Record each source as you use it and cite in the system your organisation prefers.

units.failure: important point lost in a long sentence
units.reason: A key point placed mid-way in a long explanation is easily missed.
units.rule: Vary sentence length: short sentences for plain facts, longer ones where items must be weighed against each other.

units.reason: Several paragraphs with space between invite reading where one solid block repels it.
units.rule: Use paragraphs both to keep related content together and to open up the page.

units.reason: Formal does not mean complicated, and elaborate wording distracts from the content.
units.rule: Prefer ordinary everyday words and, where policy allows, the active voice with a named agent over impersonal constructions.

units.reason: Readers may not know a shortened form and non-standard units look careless.
units.rule: Spell out an abbreviation before first using it, and use only recognised abbreviations for units.

units.reason: Automated checks miss exactly the errors that damage a technical document.
units.rule: Check spelling yourself after each section; a spellchecker passes wrong-but-real words and gives no help with technical terms.

units.reason: Readers rarely break off to hunt for a figure elsewhere, so a distant one goes unseen.
units.rule: Place each figure or table beside the text that discusses it, or in an appendix if it is only supplementary.

units.reason: Clear referencing ties each figure to the passage that needs it.
units.rule: Refer to every figure in the text and number it by section and sequence within that section.

units.reason: Space and economy make a table easier to read.
units.rule: Lighten tables: put units in the column headings, group like items, and decide whether rounded figures or fewer data would serve the reader.

units.reason: Different scales make a visual comparison misleading.
units.rule: When graphs are meant to be compared, draw them to the same scale.

units.failure: summary that needs the report to be understood
units.reason: It is the part most readers, and the most senior ones, actually read, sometimes instead of the report.
units.rule: Write the summary as a short self-contained account in continuous prose: enough background to stand alone, the main findings, and the important conclusions and recommendations.

units.failure: errors and inconsistencies in the issued report
units.reason: An error-free document is more credible, and fresh or outside eyes catch what the author overlooks.
units.rule: Have two people check the finished report, a specialist for content and logic and a non-specialist for language; let your own draft rest a couple of days before rereading.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: A Step-by-Step Guide to Writing a Compelling Feature Article

units.reason: A feature holds readers to the end only if each part does its own job.
units.rule: Build the piece in three parts: an opening that hooks, a body that delivers the substance, and an ending the reader remembers.

units.failure: a feature that opens like a news bulletin
units.reason: Readers are drawn in by people and images before they are ready for argument.
units.rule: Open with a small illustrative story or a vividly described scene instead of a summary of the facts.

units.failure: an attractive opening unconnected to the story
units.reason: A hook that leads nowhere breaks the promise it makes.
units.rule: Tie the opening to the broad subject, the specific angle and a central claim that tells the reader why the piece matters.

units.reason: Interest, not importance alone, keeps a feature reader going.
units.rule: Choose the most interesting angle, not merely the weightiest one, and anticipate the questions your intended reader would ask.

units.failure: a reader left asking what the point is
units.reason: It moves the reader from one case to the wider issue and justifies reading on.
units.rule: Directly after the opening anecdote or scene, write a paragraph that names the subject of the whole piece and its importance to the reader.

units.reason: Material that arrives late ends up jammed in where it sits badly.
units.rule: Finish the research and interviews before you start to write.

units.failure: an anecdote with no evidence of scope
units.reason: Data gives a personal story scale and credibility.
units.rule: Follow an individual's experience with figures that show how widespread the situation is.

units.reason: A good quotation can do in a line what paragraphs of explanation cannot.
units.rule: Use a well-chosen quotation from an expert or a participant where it conveys authority or an outside view more economically than your own prose.

units.reason: Shown detail keeps readers emotionally engaged.
units.rule: Describe concrete details and let readers draw the conclusion, instead of announcing the conclusion for them.

units.failure: a body that is a pile of information
units.reason: A body that reads like a list loses the reader.
units.rule: Give every paragraph a reason to be there, with something of interest in it, and make it lead logically to the next.

units.reason: A common thread ties the gathered material into one story.
units.rule: Order the body by time, by theme or by alternating viewpoints, and run a single unifying thread from the opening to the close.

units.reason: Signalled shifts keep the reader's momentum through a turn.
units.rule: Mark each change of direction with a short linking sentence or phrase.

units.failure: a body stuck at one level
units.reason: The movement keeps the piece lively and shows why the big picture matters to people.
units.rule: Alternate between the individual case and the wider picture: person, expert explanation, larger cause, then the person again.

units.failure: an ending that simply trails off
units.reason: An ending needs direction, not just a stop.
units.rule: Close by acknowledging the distance the reader has travelled, then point forward to a solution, a clear position, or a question that lingers.

units.failure: an ending unrelated to the opening
units.reason: Coming full circle gives a sense of completeness.
units.rule: Consider returning at the close to the person, image or moment from the opening, now seen with what the reader has learned.

units.reason: The subject's own words can move a reader more than the writer's summary.
units.rule: While interviewing, listen for a turning point, a lesson or a resolution; a strong closing quotation often comes from there.
