units.reason: A feature is not an essay, and a recap explains what was already explained.
units.rule: Do not finish by repeating the opening or listing the points again in order.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Mastering the Art of Writing Engaging Leads for Your Stories

units.failure: an opening that depends on the rest of the story
units.reason: Many readers stop after the first paragraph.
units.rule: Write the opening paragraph so that a reader who goes no further still knows what happened and why it matters.

units.failure: an opening crammed with every fact
units.reason: Trying to answer everything at once makes the sentence unreadable.
units.rule: Pick only the few most newsworthy of the six basic questions for the opening and hold the others for later paragraphs.

units.reason: Impatient readers need the point fast, and a short opening builds momentum.
units.rule: Keep the opening to one sentence, two at most, of roughly 25 to 40 words.

units.reason: Brevity without specifics tells the reader nothing.
units.rule: Be brief and specific together: a short opening must still name the concrete thing that happened.

units.failure: the cause held back until the last words
units.reason: That is the most natural and direct word order in English.
units.rule: Build the opening sentence in actor, action, thing-affected order.

units.failure: a passive opening that hides the actor
units.reason: Active sentences are shorter and show who did what.
units.rule: Prefer the active voice; allow the passive only when the person or thing acted upon matters far more than the actor.

units.reason: Loaded words insert the writer's opinion into a factual report.
units.rule: Leave judging adjectives and adverbs out of the opening and let the facts carry the weight.

units.reason: An unattributed opinion reads as the publication's own claim.
units.rule: Attribute to a named source any statement in the opening that expresses opinion and not settled fact.

units.failure: a slow start on urgent news
units.reason: It is the standard top of the most-important-first story form.
units.rule: For hard and breaking news, use a summary opening that answers the most critical basic questions at once.

units.failure: a striking fact diluted by lesser ones
units.reason: A single strong element lands harder than a full inventory.
units.rule: When one fact is far more striking than the rest, build the opening on that fact alone.

units.failure: an opening led by a name nobody knows
units.reason: An unfamiliar name means nothing and pulls attention from the action.
units.rule: If the person involved is unknown to readers, describe them by age or role in the opening and give the name lower down.

units.reason: News readers come for answers, and a question can feel like a gimmick.
units.rule: Avoid opening a news story with a question; keep that device for opinion or explanatory pieces.

units.failure: an opening that states the obvious
units.reason: That an event was held is obvious and not news.
units.rule: Open with what was decided or what happened, never with the mere fact that a meeting or event took place.

units.reason: A pronoun with no referent makes the reader search for the subject.
units.rule: Do not begin the opening with a vague pronoun construction; name who did what straight away.

units.reason: A forceful verb makes ornament unnecessary.
units.rule: Let forceful verbs and concrete nouns drive the opening, not decorative modifiers.

units.reason: Yesterday's angle makes the report feel stale.
units.rule: On a continuing story, open with the newest development, not with what was already known a day earlier.

units.reason: What is awkward to say is awkward to read.
units.rule: Read the opening aloud and rework it wherever you trip over the words.

units.failure: an opening that mismatches the story
units.reason: The best way in is easier to see when the story is complete.
units.rule: Consider drafting the body first and writing the opening last, once the whole shape of the story is clear.

units.reason: Each surplus word slows the reader at the most important point.
units.rule: After drafting the opening, delete every word that adds no meaning.

units.reason: Readers notice what sets a story apart, and mechanical openings lose them.
units.rule: Lead with whatever is most unusual or has the greatest impact, and vary your approach instead of reusing one stock pattern.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Academic Phrasebank | Discussing findings

units.failure: results lumped together and none properly interpreted
units.reason: Several results need several passes, and a repeated cycle keeps each one fully treated.
units.rule: Centre each part of the discussion on one stated result, and repeat the same cycle for every further result.

units.failure: a discussion that only repeats the results
units.reason: These are the elements readers most often find in a discussion, in roughly this order.
units.rule: Inside a cycle, recall the question or the literature, restate the result, flag what is notable or surprising, compare with earlier studies, explain it, then draw implications.

units.failure: overclaiming causes the data cannot prove
units.reason: An explanation of a finding is an inference, not an observation, so certainty would overclaim.
units.rule: Word explanations and implications tentatively: hedge when you say why a result occurred or what it might mean.

units.failure: findings left unconnected to the field
units.reason: Placing a finding beside prior work shows what it adds or disputes.
units.rule: Say plainly whether each result backs up or runs against what earlier studies reported.

units.failure: readers trusting a fragile result too far
units.reason: Marking the limits of a result guides how far others may rely on it.
units.rule: Tell readers where a finding should be read with caution, and close the cycle with ideas for further work.

units.failure: a one-sided case presented as a discussion
units.reason: In essays, discussion means considering competing positions, not reporting.
units.rule: When you discuss an issue instead of data, weigh both sides of the question before you arrive at a conclusion.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Academic Phrasebank | Introducing work

units.failure: an opening that never says what the essay is for
units.reason: Readers expect these moves and use them to orient themselves before the argument starts.
units.rule: Build an essay opening from a few moves: set out the background and why the subject matters, raise the problem, define terms, declare the aim, preview the layout.

units.failure: an overbuilt introduction on a small assignment
units.reason: A light introduction suits a light task and still orients the reader.
units.rule: For a simple piece, let the opening do only three jobs: name the subject, say why it matters, and show the order of what follows.

units.failure: scene-setting that eats a short word limit
units.reason: There is no room for scene-setting when the whole text is short.
units.rule: In a very brief assignment, begin directly by declaring what the piece sets out to do.

units.failure: a thesis introduction missing the gap, the aims or the map
units.reason: A thesis opening is compact but has many functions, and examiners look for each.
units.rule: Keep a thesis introduction short beside the later chapters, yet cover context, a brief look at earlier scholarship, the gap, aims and questions, method outline, value, key terms and a chapter map.

units.failure: a study presented without the gap that justifies it
units.reason: This territory, niche, occupation sequence is the pattern readers of research articles recognise.
units.rule: Move in three steps: mark out the field and its earlier work, point to what is missing there, then fill that space with your purpose, questions, value and layout.

units.failure: a formulaic introduction padded with moves it does not need
units.reason: The typical sequence is common but not fixed, and not every introduction needs every move.
units.rule: Treat the usual order of introductory moves as a default, not a law: reorder them or leave one out when the paper calls for it.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Academic Phrasebank | Writing Conclusions

units.failure: a conclusion that summarises but never judges
units.reason: A summary alone leaves the reader without the writer's final position.
units.rule: Give the conclusion two jobs: look back by drawing together the main ground covered, then offer a closing judgement on it.

units.failure: a conclusion that reopens the argument
units.reason: Its role is to consolidate, not to develop new material.
units.rule: Keep the conclusion shorter than the sections that carry the argument.

units.failure: an ending with no sense of what follows
units.reason: A forward look gives the closing judgement practical or intellectual consequence.
units.rule: Let the final comment suggest improvements or speculate about where matters may go next.

units.failure: a thesis ending with a bare summary
units.reason: Longer research writing needs a fuller closing than an essay does.
units.rule: In a dissertation, widen the conclusion: restate the aims, summarise the findings, say why they matter, admit the limits, and recommend future research.

units.failure: limitations that undercut the work's real contribution
units.reason: A limitation stated alone can make the whole study look unsound.
units.rule: When you admit a limitation, pair it with the finding or contribution that still holds despite it.

units.failure: a redundant conclusion or a missing expected one
units.reason: Conventions differ by document type, and a duplicate ending wastes space.
units.rule: In an article, drop a separate conclusion only when the discussion already consolidates the study and its wider implications; essays and dissertations normally need one.

units.failure: practical advice buried among research suggestions
units.reason: Practitioners and researchers look for different advice.
units.rule: Where findings bear on practice or policy, set those recommendations out as their own move, apart from recommendations for research.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Advanced Writing Requirement

units.reason: The school's standard asks for a position, not a summary.
units.rule: In a law seminar paper, go past describing the present law and argue what the law or policy ought to be.

units.failure: analysis that ignores facts or policy
units.reason: All three are named in the criteria the paper is judged against.
units.rule: Take up a complex legal or public-policy problem and analyse the law, the policy and the facts that bear on it.

units.reason: The criteria require engagement with the main opposing positions.
units.rule: Set out the chief competing views on the problem and analyse each of them.

units.reason: A qualifying paper must propose an answer to the problem it describes.
units.rule: Say how the issues you raised should be settled, and argue for that resolution.

units.reason: The reader must see that the argument rests on the relevant sources.
units.rule: Show command of both primary and secondary authority: cases, statutes, regulations, policy studies and empirical work.

units.failure: a compilation of other people's work
units.reason: Originality of thought is an express condition of the standard.
units.rule: Contribute analysis of your own; do not just report, compile or describe what other authors wrote.

units.failure: key facts buried among trivial ones
units.reason: The requirement names both as skills the paper is meant to build.
units.rule: Arrange the account so it is easy to take in, and separate the important facts from the minor ones.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: The inverted pyramid for news

units.failure: a news story that saves its point for the end
units.reason: News audiences want the outcome first, not the reasoning that leads to it.
units.rule: Reverse the essay order: begin with the essence of what happened rather than building towards a conclusion at the end.

units.failure: details arranged in no order of importance
units.reason: Ordering by relevance lets each reader leave when they have had enough.
units.rule: After the top line, add the consequences for those affected, then reaction, expectations and responses, each layer less essential than the last.

units.failure: a top that only makes sense with the rest
units.reason: Many people never get past the top of a story.
units.rule: Make the headline and opening summary complete enough that someone who stops there still knows the basic facts.

units.reason: Background is the part most readers can do without.
units.rule: Place background that merely supports the main thrust at the bottom, for readers who want to go deeper.

units.reason: The structure only works when the writer has ranked the material.
units.rule: Before writing, deliberately choose the single lead point and then rank every remaining point beneath it.

units.failure: getting bogged down in one aspect
units.reason: Too much of one sort of detail drives the audience away.
units.rule: Balance the kinds of information you give; do not dwell on one strand of detail while neglecting other sides of the story.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Quick Guide: Writing a news story

units.failure: a story with no news peg
units.reason: A piece with no clear reason to exist today reads as filler.
units.rule: Know the peg before writing: be able to say why this is being reported now and why this audience should care.

units.failure: key facts buried low in the story
units.reason: People who read only the top still come away informed.
units.rule: Rank the facts and put the most critical ones in the opening paragraph, with the rest following in falling order of importance.

units.failure: a report with an unanswered basic question
units.reason: Readers need each of those basics to understand an event.
units.rule: Check that the finished piece answers all six basic reporting questions (the five Ws plus how).

units.reason: One-idea sentences are easy to take in at reading speed.
units.rule: Write short, plain sentences that each carry a single idea.

units.failure: errors in names, dates or figures
units.reason: Small factual slips damage the trust the whole report depends on.
units.rule: Double-check every name, date and number before the piece goes out.

units.reason: A single-sided account is neither fair nor impartial.
units.rule: Seek out several of the people involved, so that the account reflects more than one side.

units.failure: a flat report with no voices
units.reason: Real voices make a report livelier and more credible than paraphrase alone.
units.rule: Bring in the exact words of interviewees where they add humanity or authority to the account.

units.failure: a story only insiders can follow
units.reason: Not every reader has followed earlier coverage.
units.rule: Supply enough background that a newcomer to the subject can follow the whole story.

units.reason: News reporting informs; it does not tell people what to think.
units.rule: Strip out your own views and keep to verifiable facts, leaving the judgement to the audience.

units.reason: A last pass catches padding and slips the drafting eye missed.
units.rule: Give the piece a final read to cut words that do no work and to fix spelling.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Reference documentation - Microsoft Style Guide

units.failure: entries that must each be learned afresh
units.reason: Developers look things up rather than read through, and sameness tells them where each kind of detail sits.
units.rule: Keep the layout, heading names and wording the same from one reference entry to the next.

units.failure: titles that do not say what is documented
units.reason: The kind tells the reader at once whether this is the item they were looking for.
units.rule: Title an entry with the name of the programming element followed by what kind of element it is.

units.reason: Identical titles cannot be told apart in a list of search results.
units.rule: When several elements share one name, add the owning element, product or technology to the title to tell them apart.

units.reason: A description that only rewords the name teaches the reader nothing.
units.rule: Open with one or two tight sentences on the job the element performs, or the thing it stands for, trying not to simply echo its name.

units.failure: syntax missing for the language in use
units.reason: Readers copy from this section and need the form that fits their own language.
units.rule: Show the defining code signature, and supply the syntax in every programming language the technology supports.

units.failure: calls made with wrong or missing arguments
units.reason: A caller cannot use the element correctly without knowing what each argument must be.
units.rule: Describe every parameter with its data type and, where it applies, whether callers must supply it, and whether it carries input or output.

units.reason: The name and type are already visible, so repeating them wastes the entry.
units.rule: Make each parameter description add real detail; do not just reword the parameter name or its type.

units.failure: return values the caller must guess at
units.reason: A bare type does not tell the caller what the result means.
units.rule: Describe what the element returns and its data type; for a true-or-false result, say what condition it reports.

units.failure: surprises discovered only at run time
units.reason: Important behaviour is often invisible in the syntax, parameters and return value.
units.rule: Use a remarks section for what the signature cannot show: fuller behaviour, how the element differs from similar ones, and likely pitfalls.

units.failure: reader cannot see how to call the element
units.reason: Seeing working usage is often faster than reading a description of it.
units.rule: Include a code sample that shows the element being used.

units.reason: Callers need to know what to handle and when it can happen.
units.rule: List the exceptions or errors the element can raise and the conditions that cause each one.

units.reason: Readers need to know what they get when they set nothing.
units.rule: For a field or property, describe its value and data type, and state the default when there is one.

units.reason: An element that cannot run in the reader's environment is useless to them however well described.
units.rule: State the language or platform requirements, and any security permissions, that using the element depends on.

units.reason: Reference readers move sideways between related entries.
units.rule: End with links to related elements and to further material on using this one.

units.failure: boilerplate sections with nothing in them
units.reason: Empty or forced sections add noise without information.
units.rule: Include only the sections relevant to the element at hand; which ones varies from one language or technology to another.

units.failure: raw internal comments published as documentation
units.reason: Comments are written by developers for themselves and may omit or expose the wrong things.
units.rule: When entries are generated from source-code comments, review them: add what customers need and take out internal implementation detail.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing step-by-step instructions - Microsoft Style Guide

units.reason: Numbers show the order and let readers keep their place while switching between the text and the screen.
units.rule: Set out a task that takes several actions as a numbered list, one number per action.

units.reason: A step holding several unrelated actions is easy to half-complete.
units.rule: Give every instruction its own step; merge two only when both are brief and happen at the same spot in the interface.

units.reason: Readers act as they read, so they must be looking at the right place before they are told what to do there.
units.rule: Say where an action takes place before saying what the action is.

units.failure: steps that describe instead of instruct
units.reason: A verb-first step tells the reader at once what to do.
units.rule: Begin a step with a command verb, unless a short locating phrase is needed first to put the reader in the right place.

units.failure: clipped fragments that can be misread
units.reason: Whole sentences read as complete, unambiguous instructions.
units.rule: Write each step as a full sentence, starting with a capital letter and closing with a full stop.

units.failure: readers lost before the first action
units.reason: The rest of the procedure only makes sense once the reader is in the right starting place.
units.rule: If readers could be unsure where the work is done, open with a step naming the program, tool or screen area.

units.failure: task left unfinished at the last click
units.reason: A reader who stops before the confirming action has not actually done the task.
units.rule: Carry the procedure through to its finishing action, such as confirming or applying the change, in nearly every case.

units.reason: A long run of steps discourages readers and makes it easy to lose the thread.
units.rule: Limit how many steps one procedure holds; aim for a set that can be seen whole without scrolling.

units.reason: Readers hunting for one task scan headings, not body text.
units.rule: Consider putting a brief heading above each set of instructions that names the task those instructions help the reader carry out.

units.failure: headings that read as an uneven jumble
units.reason: A steady pattern lets the eye compare headings quickly.
units.rule: Phrase all the task headings in one document to the same grammatical pattern.

units.reason: A sentence that echoes the heading delays the reader without telling them anything.
units.rule: Put a lead-in sentence before the steps only when it adds needed information; never use it to restate the heading.

units.failure: a numbered list with one item
units.reason: Numbering a lone action implies more steps are coming.
units.rule: For a task of only one action, the list format may be dropped; where neighbouring procedures are lists, mark it with a bullet, not a number.

units.failure: menu paths unintelligible in a screen reader
units.reason: The shorthand saves space for sighted readers but can run the names together when read aloud.
units.rule: A simple chain of menu choices may be compressed with angle-bracket separators, but ask an accessibility specialist first, since screen readers can skip the symbols.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Top 10 tips for Microsoft style and voice - Microsoft Style Guide

units.reason: Many readers take in only the opening of a passage.
units.rule: Put what matters most first, place key terms early for people who scan, and make the reader's choices and next action plain.

units.reason: Extra words dilute the message and cost the reader time.
units.rule: Carry the idea in as few words as it needs; when two versions say the same thing, keep the shorter.

units.reason: More detail than the decision needs slows the reader down.
units.rule: Supply just the amount of information readers need to decide with confidence, and trim every word beyond that.

units.reason: Text that sounds like friendly speech is easier to follow than formal or specialist phrasing.
units.rule: Write the way you would talk to someone, test the draft by reading it aloud, and drop jargon and needlessly technical wording.

units.reason: Contracted forms make the writing sound warm rather than formal.
units.rule: Use contractions where natural speech would use them.

units.reason: Verb-first sentences are direct, while filler openers delay the real subject.
units.rule: Start statements with a verb where you can, cut needless phrases about what the reader is able to do, and avoid empty openers that merely announce something exists.

units.reason: Sentence-style capitals are easier to read and to apply consistently.
units.rule: Capitalise headings as you would a sentence: the first word and proper names only.

units.reason: A heading is a label, not a sentence.
units.rule: Leave titles, headings and subheadings without a closing full stop or colon.

units.reason: The last comma keeps the final two items from being read as one unit.
units.rule: When a series has at least three items, put a comma before the final joining word.

units.reason: Consistent spacing keeps the text tidy and uniform.
units.rule: Put a single space after sentence-ending punctuation and after colons, and set dashes with no space on either side.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Journal Article: Abstract : Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard (MIT Communication Lab CommKit)

units.failure: an abstract the reader must reorder mentally
units.reason: A predictable sequence is what makes a compressed text clear.
units.rule: Present the parts in a predictable order: general background, specific background, the knowledge gap, your answer and approach, key methods and results, implications.

units.reason: Readers need orientation before they can value the gap.
units.rule: Spend about a sentence on the broad field and one on the specific topic, moving from wide to narrow, and briefly define any jargon you use.

units.failure: results with no question behind them
units.reason: The gap is the reason the work exists.
units.rule: After saying what is known, give one sentence to what is not known: the specific question your work tries to answer.

units.failure: a main finding buried or left out
units.reason: The reader should meet the main conclusion directly.
units.rule: In one sentence, state your overall approach and how it answers the question just raised.

units.reason: It shows how the claim was reached without the detail.
units.rule: Use one to three sentences for a high-level account of the chief methods and findings behind that conclusion.

units.failure: an abstract that stops at the data
units.reason: Readers want the significance, not only the result.
units.rule: Finish with a sentence on how the findings change understanding of the field or what they mean for later studies.

units.failure: a paper that its audience never reads
units.reason: Title and abstract are how the intended audience finds the work.
units.rule: Remember that scientists skim an abstract to decide whether the paper deserves their time, so put the work in context and describe it plainly.

units.failure: an abstract out of step with the paper
units.reason: Condensing is easier once the full argument is fixed.
units.rule: Write the abstract last, after reading the whole paper and reducing each section to its main points.

units.reason: Working by subtraction forces priorities in a tiny space.
units.rule: To choose what to report, list every finding and then strike out or merge items until only the essential ones remain.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Paper: Discussion/Conclusion : EECS Communication Lab (MIT)

units.failure: a discussion that begins as a rerun
units.reason: A strong opening claims the paper's place at once.
units.rule: Do not start by summarising results or repeating the introduction; start with what makes this paper distinctive, for instance a sentence or two tying the results to the literature.

units.reason: Readers who skipped the results still need the bottom line.
units.rule: Restate the paper's main conclusion in a sentence or two.

units.failure: results left unrelated to the motivating question
units.reason: The introduction poses the question and the discussion says how far it is answered.
units.rule: Connect the results back to the large questions the introduction raised, treating the two sections as partners.

units.failure: results floating free of the literature
units.reason: It shows what the paper extends, reconciles or contradicts.
units.rule: Say whether your findings match or contradict comparable earlier work, and explain why.

units.reason: Every study is finite, and honest bounds point to the next step.
units.rule: Explain how the limits of the study leave bigger questions open, and what would be needed to settle them.

units.reason: A paper is one contribution to a continuing conversation.
units.rule: End by looking ahead, placing the paper in the likely course of future research, as a closing statement or a subsection.

units.failure: a discussion pitched at no one in particular
units.reason: Different readers come to the discussion for different things.
units.rule: Decide for each paragraph who will find it interesting: non-experts want the high-level meaning, experts want your reading of confusing or conflicting results.

units.failure: the wrong level for the venue
units.reason: The mix of readers depends on where the paper appears.
units.rule: Balance expert and general content by venue: broad-readership outlets draw more general readers than field-specific ones.

units.failure: a discussion detached from the paper's purpose
units.reason: It reconnects the ending with the motivation.
units.rule: Consider a short reminder of why the problem matters and how your method of solving it moves the field forward.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Paper: Introduction : EECS Communication Lab (MIT)

units.failure: a reader unsure what the paper achieves
units.reason: These answers prepare and persuade the reader to continue.
units.rule: Answer four things: what problem the paper solves, why it is important or hard, how the paper solves it, and what is new.

units.failure: contributions that only full readers discover
units.reason: For those readers the introduction is the whole paper.
units.rule: Make the contribution unmistakable, since many readers stop after the introduction and want to know what was achieved and why, not how.

units.failure: an introduction only insiders can follow
units.reason: People outside the specialism often read no further.
units.rule: Pitch the introduction to a wider readership than the remaining sections, supplying general background that lets any reader follow the topic.

units.failure: a motivation the paper does not satisfy
units.reason: It guarantees that the stated problem matches what the paper delivers.
units.rule: Work out the story backwards: begin from what you did, list the contributions, find the problem they address, then motivate that problem.

units.reason: It orients the reader from shared ground to the specific gap.
units.rule: Open on a concern everyone shares, follow with specific background that credits earlier work and competing approaches, then show why this particular problem is worth solving.

units.reason: The introduction is for motivating and situating the work.
units.rule: Hold technical detail to the minimum needed to grasp the problem and the contributions; defer the remainder to later sections or a dedicated background section.

units.failure: underselling how general the work is
units.reason: A more basic question draws a wider audience.
units.rule: Pose the problem as the most basic and simple question the work answers, and do not make the results look narrower than they are.

units.reason: Readers expect some stated problem to be addressed completely.
units.rule: Let the motivation reach wider than the stated problem if you wish, but be sure the paper fully solves the problem it states.

units.failure: an introduction that misjudges the venue
units.reason: Conventions for introductions vary widely between subfields.
units.rule: Set breadth, length and structure by the target journal or conference: study successful papers there and match their level of generality.

units.failure: work that looks like a repeat
units.reason: Novelty has to be claimed explicitly to be credited.
units.rule: Name what separates your work from what already exists, and what in your solution is novel.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 21W.755 Writing and Reading Short Stories (Spring 2012), session 8 lecture notes: Plot

units.reason: Events feel caused when they come from desire meeting resistance.
units.rule: Derive the plot from three things: what the main character lacks and wants, what blocks it, and how the character tries to get past the block.

units.reason: Conflict is what turns a situation into a story.
units.rule: Make sure something really stands between the character and the wish; a narrative without that opposition is not yet a story.

units.reason: Readers stop trusting a story the moment it strains belief.
units.rule: Keep invented events plausible, even though actual life is allowed to be unbelievable; fiction is held to a stricter standard of credibility.

units.reason: The frame exists so the reader can make sense of what the character goes through.
units.rule: Treat plot as the frame that holds up character and feeling, not as the thing the story is about.

units.failure: jumbled events hiding the emotional line
units.reason: Arrangement is what makes inner experience understandable to someone outside it.
units.rule: Order the incidents so that a reader can follow what the character is living through inwardly, leading up to the story's central moment.

units.reason: Early placement lets the outcome be understood when it arrives, even if the reader had forgotten the detail.
units.rule: Supply the facts a reader will later depend on well ahead of the point where they matter.

units.reason: An ending made of known pieces feels earned and one made of new pieces feels arbitrary.
units.rule: Build the outcome from things the reader has already been shown; do not introduce a brand-new element to produce the ending.

units.reason: Too much surprise makes the close seem unbelievable.
units.rule: Prepare surprises through the details chosen earlier, so that even an unexpected ending looks reasonable in hindsight.

units.reason: That sense of rightness is what satisfies a reader of fiction.
units.rule: Aim for a close that leaves the reader feeling the result is deserved, or else one that says something wise about unfairness.

units.failure: wasted detail in a short form
units.reason: A short piece has no room for details with a single use.
units.rule: Because the form is brief, choose details that do two jobs together, such as showing who a person is while also preparing what will happen.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 21W.755 Writing and Reading Short Stories (Spring 2012), session 11 lecture notes: Point of View

units.reason: Viewpoint changes nearly everything about how the same events read.
units.rule: Decide on purpose who narrates, how much that narrator knows, and whether the reader should believe them.

units.reason: A brief form lacks the space to establish more than one consciousness.
units.rule: Hold a short piece to one viewpoint; leave movement among several characters' minds to the longer room of a novel.

units.reason: Retelling from elsewhere teaches the writer about the situation and may fix the draft.
units.rule: If a draft is stuck, rewrite part of it in another grammatical person or through a different character, even only as a trial.

units.failure: viewpoint that cannot deliver needed information
units.reason: Each choice trades intimacy against knowledge.
units.rule: Weigh a first-person teller, who gives closeness and a distinctive voice but knows little, against a third-person teller, who can notice more but stands further off.

units.failure: narrator knowing more or less than the timing allows
units.reason: Temporal distance decides what the narrator can know and what suspense remains.
units.rule: Choose how far in time the telling stands from the events: an unfolding present gives urgency without hindsight, a distant past allows comment but reveals the teller survived.

units.failure: unreliable narrator the reader cannot see through
units.reason: Without a visible reality the reader cannot detect the unreliability.
units.rule: With a narrator who cannot be trusted, let the reader see what is actually going on apart from what the narrator claims.

units.reason: The cause of unreliability is part of the meaning, not decoration.
units.rule: Show why an untrustworthy narrator is so, whether through motive, lying, ignorance or misreading, and make that discovery matter to the story's central moment.

units.reason: Each change of company changes the interaction that can occur.
units.rule: Divide the action into units defined by who is present: a new unit starts whenever a person arrives or leaves and the group changes.

units.failure: scenes that do not advance the story
units.reason: A scene with no bearing on that moment slows and blurs the story.
units.rule: Keep only scenes that carry the narrative toward its central moment and are tied closely to it.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 21W.794 Graduate Technical Writing Workshop (IAP 2019), lecture notes 5: Revision

units.reason: A bare list of topics exposes the order of ideas that full prose hides.
units.rule: Once a draft exists, write down the single topic of every paragraph in sequence and study that list to judge how the paper is organised.

units.reason: A reader can hold one subject per paragraph and loses the thread when several are packed together.
units.rule: Where the topic list shows one paragraph handling several separate subjects, divide it so that each subject gets a paragraph to itself.

units.reason: Material that does not serve the thesis dilutes the argument.
units.rule: Hold each paragraph's topic against the paper's overall claim and question any paragraph that does not help to establish that claim.

units.reason: The order in which ideas were drafted is rarely the order that argues best.
units.rule: After listing paragraph topics, ask whether a different sequence would build the claim better, and move paragraphs accordingly.

units.reason: Linking backward first lets each sentence attach to the one before it.
units.rule: Start a sentence with material the reader already knows from the preceding text and save the fresh information for its close.

units.reason: Explicit signals spare the reader from guessing how two statements relate.
units.rule: Add linking and ordering words where sentences contrast, follow in a series or enumerate reasons, so the relation between them is visible.

units.reason: A steady set of subjects makes the paragraph read as being about one thing.
units.rule: Across a paragraph, keep the grammatical subjects of the sentences on the same few things instead of shifting to a new subject each time.

units.reason: Verbs carry action more directly and with fewer words.
units.rule: Put the action of a sentence into its verb; do not bury it in a noun or adjective propped up by a weak verb.

units.reason: Readers need the subject early to interpret the detail that follows.
units.rule: Make clear what a paragraph is about no later than its second sentence.

units.reason: Checking distinct levels in turn stops attention going only to surface wording.
units.rule: When reviewing a draft, look separately at the introduction, the overall arrangement, completeness of coverage, the handling of sources, the guiding commentary and sentence construction.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Inverted Pyramid: Writing for Comprehension - NN/G

units.failure: the point saved for the end
units.reason: A reader who stops at any point still leaves with the main point.
units.rule: Order the piece from the most important information down to the least, so the conclusion comes first and background last.

units.failure: a lead that withholds the news
units.reason: Even someone who reads a single paragraph learns the substance of the story.
units.rule: Answer the basic questions of who, what, where, when and why at the very start of the story, then follow with supporting detail and background.

units.failure: stories that fall apart when shortened
units.reason: An editor fitting a length can trim from the bottom without losing essentials.
units.rule: Arrange paragraphs in falling order of importance so the story can be cut at almost any point.

units.reason: The whole structure depends on knowing what the top item is.
units.rule: Before drafting, pick the one fact readers should take away even if they read just a sentence, the one that sums up everything after it.

units.reason: Ranking keeps general readers engaged while specialists can read on for detail.
units.rule: Outline the secondary material and rank it, putting first what interests the widest audience and last the fine nuances.

units.reason: Readers who skim rely on headings to understand the page and decide where to read.
units.rule: Make the main headline and every subheading descriptive of the content beneath it.

units.reason: Scanning readers often take in only how paragraphs begin.
units.rule: Make the opening sentence of each paragraph the most important sentence in it.

units.reason: The opening words are what a scanning eye picks up.
units.rule: Start sentences with words that carry information and indicate what the rest will say.

units.reason: A summary reinforces the main takeaways for readers who go no further.
units.rule: Consider placing a short summary or a bulleted set of key points above the body.

units.failure: good structure wasted on bloated text
units.reason: The ordering helps only if the content itself is strong and concise.
units.rule: Cut information that is not needed, use straightforward language, and prefer brief paragraphs and bullet lists.

units.reason: Web readers skim and scroll only when the opening convinces them the page has what they need.
units.rule: Lead a product or service description with its main point, then the supporting details in falling order of importance.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing Digital Copy for Domain Experts - NN/G

units.failure: text with no clear target reader
units.reason: Experts quickly judge whether a text is pitched at them or at the general public.
units.rule: Decide who the audience is before writing, and let that settle which terms and concepts get explained.

units.reason: Specialists read cautiously and distrust conclusions that outrun the evidence.
units.rule: For expert readers, open with data and facts in a factual tone; leave out hype, vague claims and overstated results.

units.failure: pages either too thin or too dense
units.reason: Readers grasp the gist fast and can dig further, without the page seeming either shallow or overwhelming.
units.rule: Layer detailed material: a summary at the top, fuller detail further down, and links to supporting evidence on deeper pages.

units.reason: References back up assertions and let readers trace the evidence for themselves.
units.rule: Cite a source for any idea or information taken from elsewhere and, where possible, link to the original.

units.reason: Professionals use the date to judge relevance and tend to pass over undated pieces.
units.rule: Show a publication date on time-sensitive material and on lasting material alike.

units.failure: experts concluding the piece is not for them
units.reason: Explaining the basics signals that the piece was written for someone else.
units.rule: Do not explain a field's basic terms and concepts when every reader is a trained member of that field.

units.reason: Even experts forget seldom-used terms and lack background outside their own area.
units.rule: Still explain terms when readers are new to the field, when a term is rarely used, or when it comes from a neighbouring speciality.

units.reason: Lay wording alone can be ambiguous to a specialist.
units.rule: Where a plain description could fit more than one technical concept, give the precise technical term beside it.

units.failure: definitions that clutter or are missing
units.reason: Each reader then gets the level of explanation they need without the text talking down to anyone.
units.rule: When some readers need a definition and others do not, tuck it behind a link or pop-up so it is at hand but out of the way.

units.reason: Educated readers notice small errors and judge the whole organisation by them.
units.rule: Proofread every piece for grammar and spelling before it is published.

units.reason: Experts have no time to waste and leave when the opening says nothing.
units.rule: Keep the introduction short and substantive; a long, high-level opening with little real information reads as aimed at a general audience.

units.reason: Even in research papers, specialists go straight to the parts that interest them.
units.rule: Give expert readers summaries and subheadings too, because they scan and jump about just as general readers do.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Academic Writing: Tasks

units.failure: text written without a defined reader or purpose
units.reason: Purpose and audience determine which genre conventions apply.
units.rule: Before starting, settle why you are writing and for whom, and only then turn to the genre of text required.

units.failure: idiosyncratic organisation that confuses specialist readers
units.reason: Disciplinary readers understand most easily writing that is organised in the customary way.
units.rule: Notice the recurring organisation of texts and sections in your discipline and follow it, so that readers in the field find what they expect.

units.reason: Thinking in moves makes explicit what every stretch of text is there to do.
units.rule: Plan each section as a series of moves, each with one communicative job, and build a move from smaller steps where needed.

units.failure: treating a long document as one undifferentiated task
units.reason: Large documents are compilations of sections that are each organised differently.
units.rule: Treat a long piece such as a dissertation as several smaller jobs of writing, for example introduction, literature review and discussion, each with its own pattern.

units.failure: rigid template that ignores subject norms
units.reason: The patterns vary between fields, so copying one rigidly can misfire.
units.rule: Regard conventional section patterns as typical, not fixed, and adjust them to the practice of your own subject area.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Paragraph Structure

units.reason: Paragraphs built this way are the units from which a convincing discussion is assembled.
units.rule: Compose an academic paragraph from three elements: an opening sentence stating its subject, a claim or finding, and sentences that support that claim.

units.failure: several claims crowded into one paragraph
units.reason: Every claim needs its own support, so one claim per paragraph keeps the support focused.
units.rule: Give each paragraph a single claim, its own small thesis or result, and treat that sentence as the paragraph's core.

units.reason: A claim is only as strong as the argument or example standing behind it.
units.rule: Follow the claim with reasoning or examples that substantiate it, typically in one to three sentences.

units.reason: A short fixed budget forces each paragraph to stay on one point.
units.rule: Aim for paragraphs of about five sentences: one for the topic, one for the claim, the remainder for support.

units.reason: Very long paragraphs make the writing seem rambling and unfocused.
units.rule: Treat a paragraph of eight or more sentences as a warning that it holds more than one claim, and split it.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing Abstracts

units.failure: abstract that describes without showing worth
units.reason: Those two functions are what readers and examiners look to an abstract for.
units.rule: Use the abstract to summarise the work that was done and to show what it is worth to its discipline.

units.failure: abstract with elements out of order
units.reason: Readers expect these elements in this conventional sequence.
units.rule: Order the abstract's content as background, purpose, research problem or questions, method, results or outline of the argument, conclusions, then contribution.

units.reason: Hardly any abstract has room or need for every possible element.
units.rule: Choose only the four or five elements most relevant to the study instead of covering all eight.

units.reason: Concision is the convention, and emphasis should mirror importance.
units.rule: Give each chosen element one or two sentences, weighting space by how much that element matters in the study.

units.failure: abstract that stops at the results
units.reason: A closing statement of value is the feature all effective abstracts share.
units.rule: End every abstract on the study's conclusions, implications or contribution to its field.

units.reason: Past tense makes the research seem dated and future tense makes it seem unfinished, while present reads as complete and relevant.
units.rule: Write the abstract mainly in the simple present tense.

units.reason: The abstract's task is to direct attention to the study's contribution.
units.rule: Keep detailed limitations out of the abstract and use positive evaluative wording for what the study achieves.

units.reason: That range is the usual convention, though some sciences allow up to two pages.
units.rule: Observe any word or page limit set; otherwise keep a thesis abstract between one long paragraph and one page.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Getting Started with Plain Language - Center for Plain Language

units.failure: writing for no one in particular
units.reason: Content can only be chosen and ordered once it is clear who it serves and which tasks they have.
units.rule: Before writing, name the groups who will use the document, rank the main tasks each has, and list what they must know to do them.

units.reason: Knowing the boundaries of the audience prevents trying to serve everyone at once.
units.rule: Note the reader traits that should shape the design, and decide who the document is not for as well as who it is for.

units.reason: Readers who stop early still leave with what matters.
units.rule: Put the most important information first at every level: section, subsection and paragraph.

units.reason: Extra material distracts from what the reader came to do.
units.rule: Keep the details that help readers finish their task, and drop details that do not help, even interesting ones.

units.reason: Readers can then find what they are looking for quickly and with confidence.
units.rule: Arrange the content in a logical flow and break it into short sections that end where a reader would naturally pause.

units.failure: headings that do not match their content
units.reason: A predictive heading lets readers choose where to read without sampling the text.
units.rule: Word each heading so that readers can predict what the section under it will contain.

units.reason: Brevity without connection leaves the reader to work out how the points relate.
units.rule: Keep sentences short while still logical, and connect ideas, sentences, paragraphs and sections with transitions.

units.reason: A helpful, speaking tone is easier to understand and less off-putting.
units.rule: Adopt a conversational tone in preference to a legal or bureaucratic one.

units.reason: Readers grasp the message quickly when they recognise the words and can see who acts.
units.rule: Choose forceful, active-voice verbs and words the audience already knows.

units.reason: Matching forms make a set of items easy to scan and compare.
units.rule: Give titles and the items of a list the same grammatical form, for instance each beginning with a verb.

units.failure: links that seem to lead to the wrong page
units.reason: Readers need to recognise that they have arrived where the link promised.
units.rule: On a website, make the wording of a link match the name of the page it leads to.

units.reason: Visible structure helps readers move through the material efficiently.
units.rule: Use headings at more than one level, type treatment, white space and images as signposts that organise the information and direct attention.

units.reason: Only real readers can show whether the content can be found, understood and used.
units.rule: Test the content with people who represent the intended readers, at several points during the work and not only at the end.

units.reason: Restating and doing reveal misunderstandings that a simple opinion would hide.
units.rule: In testing, ask readers to explain key ideas in their own words and watch them try real tasks; rework the places where they stumble.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Plain Language Top Ten: Making Words Work - Center for Plain Language

units.reason: Common words are open to readers whatever their background or schooling.
units.rule: Prefer everyday words the audience will recognise over jargon and technical terms.

units.reason: Short, direct phrasing is easier to take in.
units.rule: Swap wordy stock phrases for a single word, cut words that do no work, and try splitting any sentence that feels long.

units.reason: Direct address is easier to follow and holds attention better than an impersonal passive.
units.rule: Address the reader directly in the active voice so the sentence shows who has to do what.

units.reason: Many readers skim, looking for the main points, and need to find them fast.
units.rule: Divide a complicated idea into sections and use headings, bullets and lists so the content can be scanned.

units.failure: processes explained only in dense text
units.reason: Some processes and relationships are grasped faster by eye than through prose.
units.rule: Add a chart, flowchart or other visual where it explains something better than prose would.

units.reason: A fresh reader notices confusing wording and unclear instructions the writer no longer sees.
units.rule: Where you can, have someone from outside your own team read the draft.

units.reason: A definition at first use keeps every reader on the same footing.
units.rule: If a technical term or acronym has to be used, define it where it first appears.

units.reason: What is clear to colleagues can be opaque to outside readers.
units.rule: Fit the wording, the examples and the amount of detail to who will read and what they need; drop insider language for the public.

units.reason: Positive framing tells the reader what to do rather than only what to fear.
units.rule: Where possible, frame an instruction as the action that brings the good result, not as a penalty for failing to act.

units.reason: Distance and hearing the words expose problems missed while drafting.
units.rule: Treat clarity as repeated revision: reread the draft, read it aloud, and come back to it after a break.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Your quest for a lead starts with these questions about your story

units.failure: an opening written before the story is understood
units.reason: An opening can only be sharp when the writer already knows what the piece is about.
units.rule: Before drafting the opening, pin down the basic facts of the event: the action, the people affected, the place, the time, the cause and the manner.

units.reason: Those two answers give the opening its focus.
units.rule: Boil the gathered facts down to two answers: what is new, and what the piece is fundamentally about.

units.failure: an opening that buries what readers need
units.reason: The opening serves the audience, not the reporter's notebook.
units.rule: Take the reader's seat: decide which information they need most and why the news matters to them, then open with that.

units.failure: hunting through notes instead of deciding the point
units.reason: The reporter's own grasp of the story is the quickest route to its focus.
units.rule: Question yourself as you would a source, since after the reporting you know the material better than anyone you could consult.

units.reason: Polishing the top too early eats the time the rest of the piece needs.
units.rule: Settle for a workable opening on the first draft and move on; sharpen it during revision.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: On Paragraphs (Purdue OWL)

units.reason: Readers follow organised ideas and get lost when they run together.
units.rule: Give each paragraph a single idea, and begin another paragraph once the writing moves on to a different idea.

units.reason: Long sub-points crowd out the subject they were meant to support.
units.rule: Let several small points share a paragraph only while they serve its overall subject; when any grows lengthy, expand it into a separate paragraph.

units.reason: A paragraph that drifts leaves the reader unsure what it was for.
units.rule: Keep one focus from the first sentence of a paragraph to the last; do not finish on a different matter from the one it opened with.

units.reason: Continuity of subject and form makes the logic easy to follow.
units.rule: Carry the same subject forward from sentence to sentence, and build neighbouring sentences on a similar grammatical pattern where that fits.

units.reason: These verbal ties show that the sentences belong to one line of thought.
units.rule: Tie sentences together with repeated key terms, words of like meaning, pronouns pointing back to earlier nouns, and linking words.

units.reason: An early statement guarantees the reader knows the paragraph's subject.
units.rule: Announce the paragraph's subject in a sentence placed close to its start, particularly if you are a less practised writer.

units.reason: A paragraph that cannot be summed up has no clear point.
units.rule: Test every paragraph by trying to say in brief what it is about; if that is hard, rework it.

units.reason: Very short paragraphs usually assert without developing.
units.rule: Treat a paragraph of only two or three sentences as a warning that its subject has probably not been discussed fully.

units.reason: Each of these gives the reader grounds for accepting or understanding the point.
units.rule: Develop a paragraph with means such as examples, data, what others have said, a brief story, definitions, comparison, causes, effects, analysis, description or a timeline.

units.reason: The break makes the opposition visible.
units.rule: Use separate paragraphs to set contrasting positions or pieces of information against each other.

units.reason: Pauses make dense writing easier to read.
units.rule: Break a paragraph when it has become very long or its material is difficult, to give the reader a rest.

units.failure: introduction or conclusion merged into the body
units.reason: Readers expect the beginning and the end to be marked off.
units.rule: Keep opening material and closing material in paragraphs of their own, apart from the body; either may take more than one paragraph.

units.failure: reader lost in a long document
units.reason: Such guides help readers keep their place.
units.rule: In longer pieces, insert short passages that recall what has been covered and say what comes next.

units.reason: The hand-over makes consecutive paragraphs flow.
units.rule: Close most paragraphs with a sentence or more that leads from the current idea into the following one.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing Transitions (Purdue OWL)

units.reason: Showing the connection lets readers see paragraphs working toward a larger point.
units.rule: Build a transition by pointing out how the new paragraph connects with the one before, referring back to the relevant earlier material.

units.reason: Difficulty linking is a sign of a problem in the arrangement.
units.rule: Begin a paragraph at the point where the last one stopped; if that proves very hard, ask whether the two should sit together.

units.reason: The echoed term gives the reader an obvious line of progress.
units.rule: Repeat an important term from the end of the preceding paragraph near the start of the next.

units.reason: A generic link announces a new point without relating it to the old.
units.rule: Write a link that fits only these two paragraphs; avoid an all-purpose phrase that could join any pair.

units.failure: additive transition that hides the logic
units.reason: Naming the relation is what joins the two ideas.
units.rule: Let the link state the actual relation, such as cause, sequence in time or contrast, instead of merely saying that another point follows.

units.reason: Long bridging passages delay the new point.
units.rule: Keep the link short; a handful of words is often enough to make the connection.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Tips and Examples for Writing Thesis Statements (Purdue OWL)

units.failure: thesis that mismatches the paper's purpose
units.reason: The thesis has to promise the same job the paper then performs.
units.rule: Before drafting the thesis, settle whether the paper analyses, explains or argues, because each purpose calls for a different sort of thesis.

units.reason: Analysis consists of a breakdown plus an evaluation, and readers need to be told both.
units.rule: In an analytical paper, let the thesis name the matter being taken apart and the judgement reached, and have the body explain both.

units.reason: The aim is to persuade, which requires a position and grounds for it.
units.rule: In an argumentative paper, state a debatable claim such as a judgement, proposal, causal link or reading, and back it with particular evidence.

units.failure: body that wanders from the thesis
units.reason: The reader uses the thesis as a map of what will be covered.
units.rule: In an explanatory paper, have the thesis list the aspects to be explained and then explain each one in the body.

units.reason: A broad thesis promises more than the paper delivers.
units.rule: Narrow the thesis until it covers nothing beyond what the paper really treats and can be supported with particular evidence.

units.reason: Readers look for the main point at that spot.
units.rule: Place the thesis, as a rule, as the final sentence or two of the opening paragraph.

units.failure: thesis left behind by the draft
units.reason: The thesis must describe the paper that exists, not the one first planned.
units.rule: After drafting, reread the thesis and rewrite it if the paper's subject shifted during writing.

units.reason: A stated point helps the reader know what the piece is driving at.
units.rule: Even in writing that is not analysis, explanation or argument, such as a narrative, consider stating a main point in the opening paragraph.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Assignment types

units.reason: The essay form conventionally shows its structure through the flow of argument rather than labels.
units.rule: Write a research essay as continuous prose without section headings, arranged as introduction, body and conclusion.

units.failure: essay that discusses a topic without answering the question
units.reason: The form exists to defend an answer before an informed readership.
units.rule: In a research essay, answer the question set and argue from facts, addressing peers and the wider academic community.

units.reason: Direct, ordered sentences keep an argument easy to follow.
units.rule: Keep essay prose brief and factual, prefer the active voice, and let each point lead logically to the next.

units.failure: lab report missing its standard sections
units.reason: Readers of experiments expect this fixed layout and sequence.
units.rule: Divide a lab report under headings for introduction, methods, results and discussion, describing actions and outcomes in the order they happened.

units.failure: personal or present-tense account of an experiment
units.reason: The work is finished and attention belongs on the procedure, not on the person who did it.
units.rule: Write a lab report clearly and objectively, using passive constructions and the past tense.

units.reason: Replication requires enough exact detail for someone else to follow.
units.rule: Write the lab report for peers and for researchers who may want to repeat the experiment.

units.reason: Professional readers navigate and skim reports, so signposting and a summary serve them.
units.rule: Structure a case study report with numbered section headings, a table of contents and an executive summary.

units.reason: The form's purpose is to move from assessment to advice.
units.rule: In a case study, examine the situation, identify what is working and what is not, and end with recommendations.

units.failure: academic density that loses practitioner readers
units.reason: The readership extends beyond academics and needs usable conclusions.
units.rule: Pitch a case study at professionals, policymakers and general readers, in a factual, authoritative tone that is short and simple to follow.

units.failure: review that is all summary or all opinion
units.reason: The reader needs to know what the article says before weighing a verdict on it.
units.rule: In an article review, give a short summary of the article and then your assessment of its quality, as unbroken prose without headings.

units.reason: Those are the grounds on which a piece of research stands or falls.
units.rule: Direct an article review's evaluation at how the article gathered, analysed and reported its evidence.

units.failure: review that reads as a past-tense retelling
units.reason: Present tense treats the article's claims as live and under examination.
units.rule: Write an article review using active verbs in the present tense, and keep the tone evaluative and analytic.

units.failure: generic headings that hide the themes
units.reason: Informative headings show the themes that organise the review.
units.rule: Give the sections of a literature review headings that name their content rather than generic structural labels.

units.failure: overconfident personal opinion in a review
units.reason: The reviewer's authority comes from the sources, not from personal conviction.
units.rule: Keep a literature review formal and objective; any opinion offered should be tentative and grounded in the texts reviewed.

units.failure: confusion between completed and proposed work
units.reason: Tense tells the reader what is done, what stands and what is planned.
units.rule: In a project report, shift tense with the content: present for the current situation, past for completed work, future for proposed work.

units.reason: An outside organisation expects a complete formal document with these parts.
units.rule: Assemble a project report with a title page, acknowledgements, summary, contents list, introduction and body, conclusion with recommendations, references, glossary and appendices.

units.failure: report pitched at a tutor rather than its real recipient
units.reason: The reader is an external body that will act on the report.
units.rule: Address a project report to an external body, for example a public agency or a charity-sector organisation, and keep the tone factual.

units.reason: Data is often clearer shown than described.
units.rule: In reports, show data in graphs, tables or similar visuals that add to what the prose says.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: How to write a literature review

units.failure: annotated list posing as a review
units.reason: A catalogue of sources demonstrates reading but not understanding.
units.rule: Use the literature review to build an argument that shows command of the field, not to list and summarise what was read.

units.reason: Unlike most assignments, the purpose of a review is often left to the writer to set.
units.rule: Decide for yourself what the review is for, such as justifying a research question, assessing theory or method, or weighing evidence toward a recommendation.

units.reason: Grouping by idea allows sources to be compared and combined.
units.rule: Organise the material by theme, by issue or by question instead of going through papers one at a time.

units.reason: A source whose relevance is not shown does no work for the review.
units.rule: Include only relevant works, and make plain how each one bears on the main argument.

units.reason: A narrow base gives a partial picture of the field.
units.rule: Read widely, drawing on more than one research group and more than one country or region.

units.failure: outdated review or name-dropping of landmarks
units.reason: The review must show awareness of the field's state and its landmarks without drifting off its point.
units.rule: Use current material and include the influential, much-cited studies, but only where they bear on your argument.

units.reason: Excess background delays and obscures the review's case.
units.rule: Limit background to what the reader needs to get oriented and to appreciate the argument.

units.reason: Enough examples establish the point; exhaustive listing only adds bulk.
units.rule: Be selective with evidence: to show that an assumption is widespread, cite a representative set of papers, not every one.

units.reason: Identifying these is what turns a summary into a critical review.
units.rule: Examine the literature for assumptions, limitations, weak methods, unclear points, gaps and controversies that still need addressing.

units.reason: A review is an argued text and needs the same framing as any argument.
units.rule: Arrange the review as a logical argument with an introduction, a body and a conclusion.

units.reason: Coordinating many sources into one line of reasoning rarely succeeds in a single pass.
units.rule: Map or outline the argument before drafting, then revise structure across several drafts, looking for repetition and recurring themes.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: What is a Character Arc? 3 Common Types and Examples from Fiction (Reedsy)

units.reason: These three elements drive every kind of inner journey.
units.rule: Define three things for a lead: an aim, a mistaken belief about self or world that blocks it, and the understanding needed to get past that belief.

units.reason: A perfect person has no room to develop, and readers identify with flaws.
units.rule: Give the lead genuine flaws and weaknesses that leave something to work on and overcome.

units.reason: Growth is shown by failure followed by learning.
units.rule: For an arc of growth, let the mistaken belief cause repeated failures until the lead learns, drops it and reaches the aim or a revised one.

units.reason: A steady character still needs opposition to create a story.
units.rule: For a lead who does not change, make the challenge one of keeping conviction against doubt, and let the surrounding people be the ones who change.

units.reason: The refusal to learn is what makes the fall the character's own doing.
units.rule: For a downward arc, offer the lead chances to learn and have each refused, so early gains give way to decline that also harms others.

units.reason: Change that sits outside the plot is not felt.
units.rule: Show inner change through how the person responds to obstacles and through decisions made; it may be modest but must be central to events.

units.failure: hook unrelated to the character's journey
units.reason: The transformation is the essence of what the book is about.
units.rule: Sketch the lead's transformation at the planning stage and use it when working out the book's hook.

units.failure: forcing change on a series lead
units.reason: A consistent, familiar persona is part of what readers return for.
units.rule: In a series built on a recurring investigator, a lead whose core nature stays the same from book to book is an accepted pattern.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Story Structure: 7 Types All Writers Should Know (Reedsy)

units.reason: These stages recur across most narrative models and give readers a complete experience.
units.rule: Plan five stages: ordinary life and desire ending in a triggering event, pursuit under test, a peak, its consequences, and a close.

units.reason: Without tests there is only a string of happenings that will not hold interest.
units.rule: Even in a quiet genre, include growing difficulty and a point where success looks impossible.

units.reason: A controlled finish is what makes the experience satisfying.
units.rule: Use the close to bring plot, character change and theme together and to answer the questions the narrative raised.

units.reason: Writers who break conventions well understand why the conventions exist.
units.rule: Learn the conventional shapes thoroughly before departing from them, and depart only deliberately and with a purpose.

units.reason: Those three answers identify the core that subplots attach to.
units.rule: Find the basis of the plot by asking whose book it is, what that person is after, and what stands in the way.

units.reason: A known destination gives the structure a direction.
units.rule: Decide how the book ends before arranging the rest.

units.reason: A scene with no function only fills pages.
units.rule: Before drafting a scene, know who appears, where it is set, what occurs and what it contributes: forward movement or insight into a person.

units.reason: Originality comes from the character's choices, not from the template.
units.rule: Use a structural model as support, and at each of its stages ask what this particular character alone would do.

units.reason: Writing is discovery and a plan followed rigidly flattens the result.
units.rule: While drafting, let the narrative override the plan when it calls for an unplanned scene or a change.

units.failure: no turning point into the middle
units.reason: Beginning, middle and end is the simplest dependable shape.
units.rule: In three parts: establish people, time and place; let an event force the lead irreversibly into a middle full of obstacles; then give the outcome.

units.failure: story ending at the first victory
units.reason: The final trial proves the change the journey produced.
units.rule: After the hero wins the prize, do not stop: let the win bring fresh trouble and a last test that draws on what was learned.

units.reason: Modern audiences have little appetite for purely tragic outcomes.
units.rule: In commercial fiction, expect readers to want the lead to overcome obstacles and gain some success; reserve the tragic five-part shape for dark tales.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: How to Outline a Novel in 9 Simple Steps (Reedsy)

units.reason: The book evolves during writing, and judging early stalls the work.
units.rule: Treat an outline made before drafting as a frame to start from that will change, and do not judge the ideas while making it.

units.reason: One journey gives the first outline a clear line.
units.rule: Begin the outline with a single lead and a single large problem or aim; further leads can be added afterwards.

units.reason: Importance to the character is what makes readers care.
units.rule: Choose a problem whose stakes matter greatly to the lead, whether those stakes are large or small in the world.

units.reason: That event and response set the narrative moving.
units.rule: Pin down the event at which the lead first becomes aware of the problem, then the first step taken in response.

units.reason: If the first attempt worked there would be nothing left to tell.
units.rule: Make sure the lead's first step fails or merely uncovers the next step; it must not settle the problem.

units.reason: Readers stay with someone who is visibly trying.
units.rule: Keep the lead acting and persisting toward the aim, mistakes included.

units.reason: Rising difficulty keeps tension growing.
units.rule: Plan between three and five obstacles and arrange them so each is worse than the last.

units.reason: This darkest beat is the largest obstacle and sets up the resolution.
units.rule: Somewhere in the later half, include a low point at which the aim appears completely out of reach.

units.reason: A resolution through insight differs from, and deepens, the original aim.
units.rule: To resolve the low point, compare what the lead desires with what the lead requires; the exit often lies in a new self-understanding.

units.reason: Stating the change makes the journey concrete.
units.rule: Write down how the lead begins and how the lead finishes, and name the specific thing that caused the difference.

units.reason: Parallel scenes let the reader measure the distance travelled.
units.rule: Consider pairing the first and last scenes around one place or object, shown differently, so the lead's change is visible.

units.reason: Brief movable notes are easy to rearrange.
units.rule: Summarise each key scene in a single sentence on a movable card: opening, trigger, first step, three obstacles, low point, resolution, last scene.

units.reason: The writer's grasp of the plot will have changed by then.
units.rule: When the draft is finished, repeat the outlining exercise using what was actually written.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: A Plain English Handbook: How to create clear SEC disclosure documents (chapters 3 to 6 read)

units.reason: You cannot judge what is understandable without knowing who must understand it.
units.rule: Before drafting, profile your readers: their education, their familiarity with the terminology, and how they will read and later use the document.

units.reason: Novices need the clear version most, and experts lose nothing by it.
units.rule: Where readers vary in expertise, write for the least experienced and mark basic explanations visually so experts can skip them.

units.reason: Much language is recycled from older documents without anyone knowing why.
units.rule: Challenge every item in an inherited document, and drop text nobody can show to be required or useful.

units.reason: Readers skip passages they think they have already read, and may miss something new.
units.rule: Remove repeated material unless there is a real need to say it again.

units.reason: A dense opening page discourages people from reading at all.
units.rule: Limit the cover to a few key facts and move the remaining detail inside the document.

units.failure: a summary that is a second copy of the report
units.reason: A summary that duplicates the document saves the reader nothing.
units.rule: Make the summary orient the reader and highlight the main points; do not paste in paragraphs from the body or let it grow as long.

units.reason: A detail means more when the reader knows where it fits.
units.rule: Show the overall picture first and the details afterwards.

units.reason: Readers digest information in pieces and use headings to find them.
units.rule: Break the text into sections under headings that say what each section covers; avoid vague one-word labels.

units.reason: Grouping exposes repetition and spares the reader from hunting.
units.rule: Bring related information together in one place within the document.

units.failure: agentless passives that hide who acts
units.reason: Active sentences are understood faster and show who is responsible.
units.rule: Prefer active sentences built on strong verbs; keep the passive for cases where the doer matters less than the thing acted on.

units.reason: The sentence gets shorter and the action becomes visible.
