units.rule: Where a noun hides an action behind a weak verb, turn the noun back into the verb.

units.reason: Direct address makes clear who does what and keeps the reader involved.
units.rule: Speak to the reader directly by using personal pronouns such as you and we.

units.reason: Readers understand complex material by imagining a scenario.
units.rule: Explain an abstract idea with a concrete case: one person carrying out specific actions.

units.reason: It is the easiest gain because sentence structure need not change.
units.rule: Delete words that add nothing, and swap a string of words for one that means the same.

units.failure: negative constructions the reader must decode
units.reason: The positive version is briefer and simpler to grasp.
units.rule: State things positively, and where a negative phrase has a one-word equivalent, use that word.

units.reason: The longer a sentence runs, the harder each piece of it is to understand.
units.rule: Keep sentences short; when information is complex, give the context first and then split or tabulate the details.

units.failure: terms the reader does not know
units.reason: Insiders stop noticing their own jargon.
units.rule: Swap jargon and legalese for ordinary words; define on first use any term with no plain equivalent, and have an outsider check.

units.reason: Each invented label is one more thing the reader has to memorise.
units.rule: Use defined terms and coined acronyms sparingly; when a long name must be shortened, pick an intuitive short form.

units.failure: a subject separated from its verb
units.reason: This is the natural order of English and the easiest to follow.
units.rule: Keep subject, verb and object near one another, and move qualifying phrases out of the gaps.

units.reason: The arrangement decides how much the reader must hold in mind.
units.rule: Order a conditional by its shape: one condition first; one condition with several results first, results listed; several conditions after the single result, as a list.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Documentation and Citation

units.failure: readers distrusting an unfamiliar citation manner
units.reason: Readers judge a writer's membership and trustworthiness partly by whether sources are handled in the way their field expects.
units.rule: Cite and document sources in the manner your particular readers already know, so they recognise you as belonging to their scholarly community.

units.failure: wrong citation style for the assessor
units.reason: Preferences differ between instructors, so the immediate reader's wish outranks any general default.
units.rule: Before choosing a citation style, ask the person who will assess the work which style they prefer, and ask again for each new assessor.

units.failure: submission ignoring the journal's house style
units.reason: Publications often adapt or replace the common styles, and a submission is expected to match theirs.
units.rule: When writing for a journal, follow the author instructions that journal publishes, since many keep a house style or their own style sheet.

units.failure: citation system foreign to the discipline
units.reason: Each discipline has settled on a system its readers can parse without effort.
units.rule: Match the citation system to the field: APA for social and behavioural sciences, Chicago or MLA for humanities, CSE for the sciences.

units.failure: lost or inconsistent references in a long project
units.reason: Long projects gather more sources than can be tracked reliably by hand.
units.rule: For a large or long-running research project, keep every source in a reference-management tool from the outset.

units.reason: Scholarship depends on claims being checkable against their origins.
units.rule: Attribute every borrowed idea so a reader can trace where the knowledge came from and verify that it was used correctly.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Structuring written work

units.failure: introduction that never states purpose or plan
units.reason: Moving from broad to narrow orients the reader before committing them to the paper's plan.
units.rule: Build the introduction in three steps: general background or definitions, then the topic, purpose and position, then the scope and order of what follows.

units.reason: A proportionate opening leaves the bulk of the words for the argument itself.
units.rule: Keep the introduction to roughly a tenth to a fifth of the total length.

units.failure: reader lost in an unannounced structure
units.reason: A stated route lets readers see how each part fits, while a standard layout needs no announcement.
units.rule: Close the introduction with a preview of the order of sections, unless the body follows a fixed template readers already expect.

units.reason: An opening written too early promises a paper different from the one that gets written.
units.rule: Draft the introduction only once the overall position and full structure are settled, and revise it after the body is finished.

units.reason: A repeated, recognisable shape makes each paragraph easy to follow.
units.rule: Shape a paragraph as a small essay: an opening sentence naming its subject and purpose, a developing middle, and for long paragraphs a closing sentence.

units.reason: The topic claim only becomes convincing once it is elaborated and backed.
units.rule: Develop the paragraph's opening idea in its middle through definition, classification, explanation, contrast, example or evidence.

units.failure: paragraph ending on a stray new point
units.reason: A closing sentence should consolidate and connect rather than open a fresh thread.
units.rule: Use a paragraph's last sentence to sum up or comment on what was said, show why it matters to the main topic, or lead into the next paragraph; add nothing new.

units.reason: Backward links at sentence openings let the reader carry the thread forward without effort.
units.rule: Begin each sentence with something that points back to the paragraph's main idea or to the sentence before it.

units.reason: Explicit signals tell the reader how one statement bears on another.
units.rule: Use linking words to mark the relationship between ideas, such as contrast, similarity, cause, result or addition.

units.failure: hidden structure or headings where they are not accepted
units.reason: Visible divisions show the structure at a glance, but some forms do not accept them.
units.rule: Mark sections with headings and subheadings where the discipline and the assignment type permit them.

units.reason: Ending on the wider context shows what the paper's result means beyond itself.
units.rule: Reverse the introduction's direction in the conclusion: recap the scope first, confirm the thesis or the answer to the question, then widen to significance, implications or recommendations.

units.reason: A structure derived from the task or material is easier to justify than an arbitrary one.
units.rule: Take the body's organisation from the question's wording, the subject's natural order such as time or process, or your own reading such as problem and solution.

units.reason: Structural problems are easiest to fix before prose exists.
units.rule: Sketch several alternative outlines before drafting and choose the best, because rearranging an outline is far cheaper than rearranging a half-written text.

units.reason: Material outside the purpose dilutes the line of the paper.
units.rule: Drop ideas, facts and references that do not serve the overall purpose of the piece, however interesting.

units.failure: drafting without knowing where evidence goes
units.reason: A plan this detailed means every idea has a place and its evidence is already located.
units.rule: Plan down to paragraph level: how many paragraphs, the topic of each, and the points and sources each will need.

units.reason: A grid exposes which sources speak to which theme, so the writing can combine them.
units.rule: For a large body of reading, tabulate how each source or theory relates to each planned heading before writing.

units.failure: report built on the wrong template
units.reason: The middle of a report varies widely with its type and purpose.
units.rule: Before structuring a report, find out exactly which kind is expected, since the word covers many forms across disciplines.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Types of academic writing

units.failure: describing when the task asks for argument
units.reason: Each kind of writing has a different purpose, and the verbs reveal which one is being assessed.
units.rule: Read the task's instruction verbs to decide whether it wants description, analysis, persuasion or critique, and write to that level.

units.reason: Analysis consists of reorganising information, not just reporting it.
units.rule: Regroup the facts into categories, parts or relationships, give each grouping a name, and devote each paragraph and each section to a single grouping.

units.reason: A point of view persuades only when every step is supported.
units.rule: Back each claim with evidence, for instance published studies or data, that is convincing and bears directly on the claim.

units.failure: scattered points with no overall argument
units.reason: Separate points persuade only when they add up to a single coherent case.
units.rule: Make all individual claims work together toward one overall position, with the reasoning behind each made plain to the reader.

units.failure: argument resting on an invalid assumption
units.reason: A case built on a weak assumption fails even when the evidence is good.
units.rule: Check that the assumptions your argument rests on are sound before presenting it.

units.reason: Breaking a stance into parts supplies both the structure and the support for the argument.
units.rule: Divide your position into component aspects and list the reasons and kinds of evidence for each before writing.

units.failure: judging a work without representing it fairly
units.reason: A fair evaluation depends on the reader seeing what is being evaluated.
units.rule: In a critique, first summarise the work accurately, including its main interpretations, assumptions or method, before judging it.

units.reason: Critical writing requires the writer's own view set beside the author's.
units.rule: Take a clear stance on the work: identify problems, propose a better alternative, or defend it against others' objections.

units.reason: An opinion about a work carries weight only when it is substantiated.
units.rule: Support your judgement with the kind of evidence the discipline accepts, such as logical reasoning, authoritative sources or research data.

units.failure: review that lists studies without evaluating them
units.reason: The review exists to show where new research is needed.
units.rule: Write the literature review critically, judging what earlier studies do well and badly, so that a gap or opportunity becomes visible.

units.reason: That section's job is to report procedure rather than to argue.
units.rule: Write the methods section mainly as description, summarising how the information was gathered and analysed.

units.reason: This is the section where analysis and persuasion are expected.
units.rule: In the discussion, tie the findings back to the research questions and then argue for your interpretation of them.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Executive Summaries | University Writing Center

units.reason: The reader uses the summary to decide, not to learn the method.
units.rule: Write for a manager who wants costs, productivity and efficiency, not the technical detail of the project.

units.failure: a summary that never says what to do
units.reason: What concerns an executive most is outcomes and effects on the organisation.
units.rule: End with explicit recommendations grounded in the report's results; expect this part to be the longest, and keep giving specific figures in it.

units.failure: an academic abstract handed to a business reader
units.reason: That emphasis is what separates an executive summary from an abstract.
units.rule: Give most weight to results and conclusions, where an abstract might share space evenly among problem, method, results and conclusions.

units.failure: a slow start that loses the reader
units.reason: Space is short and the reader wants the problem at once.
units.rule: Skip an elaborate introduction; a single attention-catching sentence that establishes the problem is enough, and works best when you aim to persuade.

units.reason: A problem only motivates action when its stakes are concrete.
units.rule: After introducing the problem, give its particulars and explain the benefit of dealing with it.

units.reason: Method is secondary to outcome for this audience.
units.rule: Present the solution after the problem, and describe methods only if they mattered to reaching it or matter to executive readers.

units.reason: Specifics persuade and can be checked.
units.rule: Prefer concrete figures and specific claims to general statements of optimism.

units.reason: Candour about risk builds trust in the proposal.
units.rule: Do not hide possible problems or limits; say briefly how each is being handled or can be reduced.

units.reason: The summary must be a faithful miniature of the document.
units.rule: Include nothing in the summary that the full report does not itself cover.

units.reason: A condensed text needs its own wording to read well.
units.rule: Compose fresh sentences instead of pasting from the report, and drop long transitions and examples to save words.

units.reason: The reader may not be a specialist.
units.rule: Keep specialist vocabulary out, giving a short definition for any term that is unavoidable.

units.failure: a summary too long to read quickly
units.reason: That is the customary scale, longer than an abstract.
units.rule: Aim for a page or two at double spacing, roughly a twentieth of the full report's length.

units.failure: missing information that blocks the decision
units.reason: The summary exists to support a decision.
units.rule: Test the draft by asking whether it gives a decision-maker everything needed to change a policy, take an action or spend money.

units.failure: a summary out of keeping with its report
units.reason: It accompanies the report and should read as part of it.
units.rule: Place the summary ahead of the report or proposal it accompanies, and match that document's formal tone.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Literature Reviews | University Writing Center

units.failure: research that seems to come from nowhere
units.reason: The review establishes the writer as a competent contributor.
units.rule: Show how your question and your findings fit an ongoing scholarly conversation, so readers see that you know the field.

units.reason: A story links the sources and shows where knowledge stands.
units.rule: Do not list sources in arbitrary order with a summary of each; build a narrative of how the works together add to understanding.

units.failure: a review that forgets the study it serves
units.reason: Among so many sources a writer can forget the study the review is for.
units.rule: Keep your own project at the centre while you review what others have written.

units.failure: an incomplete or lopsided account of the field
units.reason: These three give a balanced and thorough picture of the conversation.
units.rule: Cover the main ideas in circulation, the most relevant or recent research, and the points most in dispute.

units.reason: Selective sourcing misrepresents the state of research.
units.rule: Choose sources that represent the whole conversation on the topic; do not pick only those that favour your own argument.

units.failure: a review with no stated stakes
units.reason: Readers need a reason to care before they follow the survey.
units.rule: Make clear to your audience why the topic deserves their attention.

units.failure: a review whose direction is unclear
units.reason: Readers follow a long survey better with the point and plan in hand.
units.rule: In the opening, name the topic, state the central point of your research narrative, and signal how the body is arranged.

units.failure: sources presented with no ordering principle
units.reason: Each scheme groups sources in a way that exposes a pattern.
units.rule: Arrange the body by trend over time, by theme, or by research method, whichever suits the story.

units.reason: The ending connects the survey to your contribution.
units.rule: Finish by summing up how your interests line up with the wider conversation, or by proposing the research needed next.

units.reason: The same logic holds at smaller scale.
units.rule: When the review is a section inside an article, keep the introduction, body and conclusion shape in compressed form.

units.reason: Synthesis is what distinguishes a review from a set of notes.
units.rule: Summarise, compare and appraise sources, then synthesise: trace how the conversation developed, expose gaps your work can fill, or show a dispute your work can help settle.

units.failure: a review that ignores disciplinary conventions
units.reason: Expectations for reviews vary between fields and document types.
units.rule: Study a published review of the same type in your own field as a model, and follow that field's citation style.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Memos | University Writing Center

units.reason: Busy readers decide in the first lines whether to keep reading.
units.rule: Open the body with your purpose so readers grasp at once what the memo contains and why it concerns them.

units.failure: making readers wade through background first
units.reason: Readers who know the topic get what they need immediately.
units.rule: By default, order ideas from most to least important: main point first, supporting facts next, background last.

units.failure: blunt bad news that is rejected or misread
units.reason: Preparation helps an unwelcome or unfamiliar message to be understood.
units.rule: For bad news, or an idea the reader must be prepared for, build up step by step and place the main point at the end.

units.failure: a memo that prompts no action
units.reason: Readers act when they know precisely what is wanted and by when.
units.rule: End with a polite, exact request for action that says what result you expect, with a deadline where useful.

units.reason: Distribution and tone both depend on who is reading.
units.rule: Send the memo only to those who need it, and set the level of formality by whether readers are supervisors, peers or subordinates.

units.reason: Explaining the familiar wastes limited attention.
units.rule: Leave out background your colleagues already have; they know the organisation's projects and vocabulary.

units.reason: You are addressing colleagues, and inflated language sounds pompous.
units.rule: Write short, active sentences in a cordial, plain, conversational manner; avoid showy vocabulary, jargon and tangled syntax.

units.reason: A written memo can travel beyond its first audience.
units.rule: When a memo complains or reprimands, choose words with care, since it may be read by people you did not have in mind.

units.failure: a memo that cannot be filed or routed
units.reason: The standard block tells readers who, when and what before the text.
units.rule: Begin with a heading block giving date, recipient, sender and subject, with an optional line for those receiving copies.

units.failure: a vague subject that gets the memo ignored
units.reason: It often decides how the memo is filed and whether it is read at all.
units.rule: Make the subject line short, and make it describe the content accurately.

units.failure: a cluttered or impolitic recipient line
units.reason: Order among names carries meaning inside an organisation.
units.rule: List a few recipients alphabetically or by rank, and name a large group by its class instead of listing everyone.

units.failure: a memo from or to an unidentified person
units.reason: Identification ensures delivery and recognition.
units.rule: Add a job title or department after a name when the reader may not know the person or the memo might go astray.

units.failure: a long undivided block of text
units.reason: Brevity and signposts serve readers short of time.
units.rule: Keep a memo brief, usually under a page; once it runs beyond two or three paragraphs, add bold headings that name each part's topic.

units.failure: a long memo that starts cold
units.reason: A longer document needs some context before its points.
units.rule: In a memo longer than a page, the first paragraph may be given to background.

units.failure: a one-way announcement with no route for reply
units.reason: It shows you are engaging readers and not just issuing a notice.
units.rule: Close by inviting questions or feedback and giving contact details; no sign-off salutation is needed.

units.reason: Attachments can become separated from the memo.
units.rule: Name any attached documents at the foot of the memo.

units.reason: This is the expected business layout.
units.rule: Set the text single-spaced in flush-left block paragraphs with a blank line between paragraphs.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: The Book Review or Article Critique | Writing Advice

units.failure: a book report in place of a critique
units.reason: A critical review is judged on its assessment, not on retelling.
units.rule: Judge the work and comment on it against your course's issues and theory; do not let summary become the main business.

units.failure: drifting into an essay on the topic itself
units.reason: It keeps the review on how the book treats its topic.
units.rule: Make the work, not its subject, the focus of your key sentences: report what the author argues or shows, not facts about the topic.

units.failure: summary and judgement tangled without plan
units.reason: Both are accepted, and a deliberate choice keeps the review coherent.
units.rule: Choose one of two shapes: summarise first and then evaluate, or comment throughout and use summary only as illustration, as your instructor directs.

units.failure: judging a work against aims it never had
units.reason: Evaluation needs a fair account of what the author set out to do.
units.rule: Identify what exactly the work is about, its apparent purpose, its intended readers and its thesis, and note whether its theoretical assumptions are stated openly.

units.reason: Concrete reference lets the reader test your judgement.
units.rule: Describe the kind of material the work presents and show how it is used to argue the thesis, pointing to particular passages to convey the author's manner.

units.reason: Testing an argument against rivals reveals its limits.
units.rule: Ask whether the same material could be argued another way, and whether the author shows awareness of those alternatives.

units.reason: A review places a work in its intellectual conversation.
units.rule: Say what the work adds to the wider subject of your course and discipline, and what questions it opens for further discussion.

units.reason: The reviewer's reasoned position is part of what the genre asks for.
units.rule: Include your own reactions, given as considered opinion.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: The Lab Report | Writing Advice

units.failure: a data dump with no sign of comprehension
units.reason: The report is meant to demonstrate understanding, not only record numbers.
units.rule: Go beyond presenting data: show that you grasp the concepts behind it by explaining how and why observed results differed from expected ones.

units.failure: readers hunting for a missing or misplaced part
units.reason: A known format lets readers find each kind of information quickly.
units.rule: Keep the usual sequence of parts, from title and abstract through introduction, materials, procedure, results and discussion to conclusion, references and appendices, adapting it to the course.

units.reason: The title should tell a reader what was done.
units.rule: Give a plain, informative title of under ten words that names the experiment, not just the lab number.

units.failure: an abstract that omits results or conclusions
units.reason: It must let a reader decide whether the full report is needed.
units.rule: Write the abstract as one paragraph of at most 200 words covering purpose, key results, the weightiest discussion point and the major conclusion.

units.failure: a copied manual standing in for understanding
units.reason: The introduction shows you understand the problem being examined.
units.rule: State the objective in a sentence or two, then supply whatever theory or formulas a reader requires, in your own understanding, not by repeating the manual.

units.reason: The experiment is over, while the report, the laws and the instruments still exist.
units.rule: Use the past tense for the experiment you carried out and the present tense for the report itself, for theory and for permanent equipment.

units.reason: Completeness matters here more than prose.
units.rule: Present materials and equipment as an accurate, complete list, or point to the standard procedure where that is permitted.

units.failure: an idealised procedure that hides deviations
units.reason: Reproducibility depends on what was actually done, not on what was planned.
units.rule: Narrate each step in its true sequence, recording every departure from the set procedure, so that someone else could repeat the work.

units.reason: Readers need to be told the finding, not left to extract it.
units.rule: State every significant result in a sentence, even when tables, figures and calculations carry the numbers.

units.failure: unlabelled graphics the reader cannot interpret
units.reason: A pointer gives the reader a focus when reading a graphic.
units.rule: Number and title each table and graph, label it clearly, and introduce it with a brief pointer to what matters.

units.failure: pages of calculation swamping the results
units.reason: One worked case proves the method without burying the findings.
units.rule: Show a single sample calculation in the body and move the remaining calculations and raw data to appendices.

units.failure: speculation mixed in with established findings
units.reason: Separating analysis from interpretation keeps firm findings apart from inference.
units.rule: First say what the results show with certainty, then interpret: their significance, the ambiguities, the questions raised and reasoned accounts of anything wrong in the data.

units.reason: Named causes show understanding, and a vague one suggests carelessness.
units.rule: Compare expected with obtained results and account for differences with specific causes; never fall back on a vague appeal to human error.

units.reason: Error analysis shows judgement about the reliability of the results.
units.rule: Analyse experimental error: say whether it was avoidable or came from equipment, and if the design was at fault, how the design could be improved.

units.failure: results never related to the purpose
units.reason: The experiment exists to test or demonstrate a principle.
units.rule: Tie the results back to the theory the lab was meant to illustrate and to the objectives you stated.

units.reason: A justified statement of the outcome is a sufficient ending.
units.rule: Keep the conclusion brief: state what is now known for sure and the evidence that justifies it; significance and further work are optional additions.

units.reason: Unreferenced appendices are never read.
units.rule: Put one kind of material in each appendix and mention every appendix somewhere in the report's body.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: The Literature Review: A Few Tips On Conducting It | Writing Advice

units.reason: A controlling concept turns a pile of summaries into a piece of reasoning.
units.rule: Organise the whole review around one guiding idea, such as your research aim, problem or thesis, and not around the sources one by one.

units.reason: Author-led paragraphs signal a list, while theme-led ones signal synthesis.
units.rule: Avoid starting one paragraph after another by naming a scholar; build each paragraph on a theme or a trend.

units.reason: The reader wants a judged account of the field, not an inventory.
units.rule: Tell readers what is established about the topic and where the strong and weak points of that knowledge lie.

units.failure: no clear picture of the state of knowledge
units.reason: That summary is what lets the review define the research question.
units.rule: Synthesise the findings into a statement of what is known and what remains unknown.

units.failure: a review that hides disputes and gaps
units.reason: Controversies and open questions are where new work finds its place.
units.rule: Point out where scholars disagree, and frame the questions that still need research.

units.failure: summary with no comparison between sources
units.reason: Comparison along shared concepts is what makes the analysis critical.
units.rule: Follow a set of concepts through the sources, comparing how each handles them and weighing strengths against weaknesses.

units.reason: Leaving out opposing work makes the review partial and less credible.
units.rule: Cite and discuss studies that run against your own view.

units.failure: too few, too many or off-topic sources
units.reason: Scope must match the task for the review to be both complete and manageable.
units.rule: Search widely enough to catch the relevant material and narrowly enough to drop the irrelevant, and fit the number of sources to the paper's length.

units.failure: treating every published result as equally reliable
units.reason: A finding is only as strong as the study behind it.
units.rule: When judging a study, check its design, the soundness of its measurements, whether the analysis fits the question, and whether the conclusions follow from the data.

units.reason: Grouping and framing show relationships that separate entries cannot.
units.rule: In an annotated bibliography, frame the entries with an opening and a close that state the scope and the question, and group entries into sections with short lead-ins.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Office of the Parliamentary Counsel: Drafting Guidance (Parts 1 to 3 read; linked from gov.uk/government/publications/dr

units.reason: People understand a part better once they know why they are being told it.
units.rule: Lead the reader through the legislation as you would explain it aloud, and consider opening with a summary of the entire text.

units.failure: a text that sends the reader back and forth
units.reason: Cross-references are hard work for a reader.
units.rule: Order the material so later propositions build on earlier ones, and reorder to reduce the need for cross-references.

units.failure: artificial structure that draws attention to itself
units.reason: The reader cares about the legal effect, not the machinery of the document.
units.rule: Let the divisions of the text follow the divisions of thought, and create no more Parts or Chapters than you need.

units.reason: The reader should learn quickly what subject the clause deals with.
units.rule: Put the main proposition of a clause at its start instead of in the middle.

units.failure: conditions stacked ahead of the point
units.reason: The reader then knows what the conditions are conditions for.
units.rule: Where a legal effect depends on several conditions, state the effect first and the conditions after it.

units.failure: overlong sentences, or a proposition scattered in pieces
units.reason: Short sentences ease the load on memory, yet fragments can obscure one thought.
units.rule: Aim for one idea a sentence, but keep a single complex proposition whole if splitting it would force the reader to reassemble it.

units.reason: Excess emphasis distracts from what the law does.
units.rule: Keep a moderate, even tone: firm without shouting, brief without being brusque, and without needless emphasis.

units.failure: a condition wedged between subject and verb
units.reason: Simple logical construction is easiest to follow.
units.rule: Build sentences as subject, verb, object, and keep other words from coming between a subject and its main verb.

units.reason: Positive wording is usually understood more readily.
units.rule: Prefer the positive statement, give quantities in positive terms, and avoid double negatives; keep a negative where a prohibition is the natural form.

units.reason: The active form is generally grasped faster.
units.rule: Prefer the active voice; use the passive where the agent is unimportant, unknown or could be anyone.

units.reason: The verb is crisper and understood at once.
units.rule: Use a verb in place of a verb-plus-noun phrase with the same meaning.

units.failure: inconsistent or archaic words of obligation
units.reason: The office treats it as a usage to avoid, while matching an existing text keeps that text consistent.
units.rule: Avoid the legislative "shall", except where you are inserting text into an enactment that already uses it.

units.reason: Language should not call attention to itself.
units.rule: Write modern standard English: no archaisms, no legal or policy jargon, and no novel fashionable words either.

units.failure: an unfamiliar word where a common one would serve
units.reason: Familiar wording reaches more readers, but accuracy must not be traded for it.
units.rule: Between two acceptable words choose the more everyday one, provided it conveys the meaning just as well.

units.reason: Opaque general words make readers lose the thread and may miss the intention.
units.rule: Where a precise meaning is intended, use the precise word, not a broad term that covers many meanings.

units.failure: gendered pronouns, or letter labels that hinder reading
units.reason: A letter is not normal English and makes the reader substitute the real noun each time.
units.rule: Draft gender-neutrally by repeating the noun, changing the pronoun or rephrasing; use a letter to stand for a person only sparingly.

units.failure: headings that do not reveal the contents
units.reason: Headings are the means by which people locate the provision they want.
units.rule: Make each heading show the contents as fully as it can on one line, and re-read the contents list to check that the headings tell the story.

units.failure: an overview that changes the meaning or adds nothing
units.reason: A court might otherwise give the overview a legal effect nobody intended.
units.rule: Add an overview only where it helps navigation; keep it accurate, plainly a signpost, and more than a repeat of the headings.

units.failure: a wall of text, or text chopped too finely
units.reason: Large blocks are hard to understand, yet fragments distract.
units.rule: Break up any slab of unbroken text longer than about six lines, but do not over-paragraph so that the sentence loses its flow.

units.failure: a list whose items combine ambiguously
units.reason: The reader should not have to reach the end to learn how the items combine.
units.rule: Make clear whether listed paragraphs all apply together or are alternatives, never mix conjunctions in one list, and move trailing words up into the opening.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Essentials for Drafting Clear Legal Rules (2024 ed.)

units.failure: wording that survives a friendly reading only
units.reason: Someone accused of breaking it will look hard for a reading that lets them off.
units.rule: Draft a rule so it cannot be misread, not merely so it can be understood.

units.failure: several phrasings for the same concept
units.reason: Unexplained variation invites the argument that a different meaning was intended.
units.rule: Use one term for one meaning and a different term for a different meaning, throughout the whole set of rules.

units.reason: A needless plural lets someone argue that the rule demands at least two.
units.rule: Draft in the singular unless the sense is unavoidably plural.

units.reason: A rule is treated as speaking continuously while it is in force.
units.rule: Use the present tense by default; keep the past for an event that must already have happened and the future for a contingency.

units.reason: The preference serves clarity and is not an absolute rule.
units.rule: Prefer the active voice, but keep a passive where the actor is obvious or unimportant, or where the active would shift emphasis or break continuity.

units.failure: conditions piled up ahead of the verb
units.reason: Placement decides whether the reader is misled on the way through the sentence.
units.rule: Lead with a short condition; lead with the main clause when it is short and the condition lengthy; list several conditions vertically after the main clause.

units.failure: a tangled subject concealing a condition
units.reason: An explicit condition is easier to see and to apply.
units.rule: Bring a condition hidden inside a long subject into the open by restating it with "if".

units.failure: a long exception delaying the rule
units.reason: The exception should sit where the reader takes it in with least effort.
units.rule: State a brief exception at the start only if the sentence would mislead without it; otherwise put it last or give it a sentence to itself.

units.reason: Interruptions delay the core of the sentence.
units.rule: Do not interrupt a subject and its verb, or a verb and its object; move the phrase, or if it must stay, set it off with paired dashes.

units.reason: Shorter sentences are easier to consult quickly and to study closely.
units.rule: Keep average sentence length below about twenty-five words by breaking compound sentences, even if a new sentence then starts with a conjunction.

units.failure: a sentence trailing off in minor detail
units.reason: A sentence's final position is where emphasis naturally falls.
units.rule: Arrange a sentence so it finishes on the word or phrase that deserves the stress.

units.reason: Positive form removes double negatives.
units.rule: Prefer a positive statement to a negative one, and turn a prohibition-plus-exception into a permission limited by "only if".

units.reason: A logical order makes the rules easy to refer to.
units.rule: Order provisions so the general precedes the specific, the widely applicable precedes the narrow, and the more important precedes the less.

units.reason: Headings give readers their bearings.
units.rule: Give every structural part an informative, accurate heading, and lean toward more headings instead of fewer.

units.failure: items listed inside a block paragraph
units.reason: A vertical list reinforces meaning and prevents syntactic ambiguity.
units.rule: Set parallel or related items out as a vertical list placed last in the sentence, never at its start or middle.

units.reason: Text with no designation cannot be cited and its scope is unclear.
units.rule: Do not leave unnumbered text hanging after a list; give it a subdivision of its own or reorder the sentence.

units.reason: Placed there, it appears to qualify one item only.
units.rule: Keep out of any single list item material that applies to the entire list.

units.reason: The text gets shorter and says more plainly who does what.
units.rule: Cut every surplus word, thin out prepositional phrases, and turn abstract nouns back into verbs, without departing from natural idiom.

units.reason: "Shall" is used in several senses, which breeds dispute.
units.rule: Fix the meaning of each word of authority and keep to it; swap "shall" for "must" or "may", or for a verb in the present tense.

units.reason: A list of instances risks an accidental omission, and intensifiers add little or weaken the point.
units.rule: Do not state the obvious, do not list every instance of a general term, and be wary of intensifiers.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: 3. The Abstract - Organizing Your Social Sciences Research Paper - Research Guides at University of Southern California

units.failure: an abstract missing design, findings or conclusions
units.reason: A prescribed order lets readers find each element at once.
units.rule: Follow a set sequence in one paragraph of at most about 300 words: purpose and problem, study design, main findings, then interpretation and conclusions.

units.failure: a teaser that says nothing of the findings
units.reason: Readers use it to decide whether the paper is worth reading.
units.rule: Include enough key results that a researcher who could reach only the abstract would still get the whole story of the study.

units.failure: a descriptive outline where an informative abstract was wanted
units.reason: The types differ in length and in what they must contain.
units.rule: Decide which kind you are writing: descriptive, which only says what the work contains, or informative, the usual kind, which also gives results, conclusions and recommendations.

units.reason: You are reporting a study that is already finished.
units.rule: Use the active voice where you can, write concise but complete sentences, and keep to the past tense.

units.failure: an abstract that describes a paper never written
units.reason: It can only summarise a paper that exists.
units.rule: Although it stands first, compose the abstract last, drawing material from every part of the finished paper and then smoothing the result.

units.reason: Short sentences carry more information in fewer words.
units.rule: Prefer short sentences to long clauses strung together with conjunctions.

units.failure: an abstract that contradicts the paper
units.reason: Late revisions often leave the abstract out of date.
units.rule: Before submitting, check that everything in the abstract agrees completely with the paper.

units.failure: an abstract that ends on raw results
units.reason: The reader should leave knowing what the study means.
units.rule: Use the final sentences for conclusions, implications or applications, followed where fitting by a note on further research the findings call for.

units.reason: An abstract informs; it does not advertise.
units.rule: Do not open with a catchy phrase, a provocative quotation or any other attention-getting device.

units.reason: Space belongs to the study itself.
units.rule: Leave long passages of background and context out of the abstract.

units.failure: an abstract that depends on material elsewhere
units.reason: The abstract has to stand alone, apart from the paper.
units.rule: Include no citations or mentions of other literature, and no figures, tables or references to them.

units.reason: Many readers see only the abstract and come from other specialisms.
units.rule: Avoid acronyms, abbreviations and jargon that could confuse a reader.

units.reason: Every word must carry information.
units.rule: Cut redundant phrases, needless adverbs and adjectives and repeated information, and never trail off or use incomplete sentences.

units.reason: These are the usual formatting expectations.
units.rule: Format it as a single block paragraph with no indentation, and report statistics in parentheses.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: 4. The Introduction - Organizing Your Social Sciences Research Paper - Research Guides at University of Southern Califor

units.failure: a problem stated before the reader can place it
units.reason: Moving from general to particular prepares the reader to understand the problem.
units.rule: Shape the introduction as a funnel: the broad subject first, then narrower context, arriving at the research problem and the reason for studying it.

units.failure: an introduction that leaves the purpose unclear
units.reason: These are the questions a reader brings to the opening.
units.rule: Make the introduction tell the reader what you studied, why it mattered, what was known before, and how the study advances understanding.

units.failure: no visible reason for the study
units.reason: This is the general outline that research introductions follow.
units.rule: Proceed in three moves: establish the research area, identify a niche such as a gap or a challenged assumption, then place your study in it with its intent, features and results.

units.reason: A map helps readers follow the argument.
units.rule: Close the introduction with a brief paragraph describing how the remainder of the paper is organised.

units.failure: an introduction that promises a different paper
units.reason: Outcomes are unknown until the study is complete.
units.rule: Return to the introduction once the body is written and revise it so that it matches the final paper.

units.failure: readers faulting the study for omissions it chose
units.reason: Explicit boundaries answer the reader who asks why something was not examined.
units.rule: State the delimitations near the end of the introduction: what the study deliberately leaves out, and why.

units.reason: They are different things and belong in different places.
units.rule: Keep delimitations, the design choices made at the start, distinct from limitations discovered once the research was done.

units.reason: It fixes the subject quickly and stops the opening being too general.
units.rule: Bring key words of the title into the opening sentences of the introduction.

units.failure: an introduction swollen into a literature review
units.reason: The reader needs only what was known about the problem beforehand.
units.rule: Give a short, balanced review of the foundational literature, with citations, and save the comprehensive review for its own section.

units.failure: purpose and method left to inference
units.reason: Purpose and approach are the core of what the reader must take away.
units.rule: State clearly the hypothesis or purpose you investigated, and follow it, in the last paragraph, with the rationale for your chosen design.

units.failure: an opening that is all flash
units.reason: One device gains attention, while several look like show over substance.
units.rule: Engage the reader with one device only: a story, a strong quotation or anecdote, a provocative question, a puzzle, or a telling example.

units.reason: A general dictionary lacks authority and the discipline's sense of the term.
units.rule: Do not open with a dictionary definition; where a definition is needed, take it from a subject-specific reference work.

units.reason: The opening needs only enough history to ground the problem.
units.rule: Keep historical context brief, starting at the point in time that shows why the study matters; put any long history in the literature review.

units.reason: A vague or error-filled start colours how the findings are received.
units.rule: Write the opening with care, because it forms the reader's first judgement of your logic, style and research quality.

units.failure: a study with no stated significance
units.reason: Readers want to know what the work is good for beyond itself.
units.rule: Note what the research contributes and implies more widely, for theory, for evidence or for policy.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: 5. The Literature Review - Organizing Your Social Sciences Research Paper - Research Guides at University of Southern Ca

units.failure: a review with no overview, grouping or verdict
units.reason: These parts together support understanding of the research problem.
units.rule: Outline the subject and the review's objectives, sort the works into categories, explain how each resembles and differs from the others, and conclude which contribute most.

units.failure: a date-ordered list with no ideas
units.reason: Thematic grouping exposes patterns that a date order hides.
units.rule: Organise by theme as the default in the social sciences, around topics or issues; time may still order the material inside a theme.

units.reason: Date order means something only if development followed it.
units.rule: Use chronological order only when the research clearly builds stage upon stage and the sequence itself shows a trend.

units.failure: headings unrelated to the review's logic
units.reason: Headings then mirror the logic of the review.
units.rule: Let subsections come from the organising principle: time periods for a chronological review, subtopics for a thematic one.

units.failure: a patchwork of other writers' voices
units.reason: Your voice has to stay in front even while presenting others' ideas.
units.rule: Open and close every paragraph in words and thoughts of your own, weaving the references into the middle.

units.reason: Summary alone does not show how the sources connect.
units.rule: After recapping a study's important features, synthesise: restate its significance and connect it with your study and with other research.

units.reason: A review is held to the same standard of evidence as any research writing.
units.rule: Support each interpretation you make of the literature with citations.

units.reason: Peripheral detail blurs the focus of the review.
units.rule: Be selective: take from each source only the points that bear directly on the research problem.

units.reason: Long quotation replaces your own analysis.
units.rule: Quote sparingly: only for emphasis, for a term the author coined, or for wording that cannot easily be paraphrased.

units.reason: A paraphrase remains another person's idea.
units.rule: Paraphrase accurately, in words of your own, and still cite the source.

units.reason: Critical evaluation, not acceptance, is the task.
units.rule: Evaluate each work on the author's credentials and evidence, the fitness of its methods, its even-handedness, its persuasiveness and its real contribution.

units.reason: Secondary accounts may be only loosely tied to the original research.
units.rule: Include relevant primary studies and data; do not rely only on secondary analyses.

units.reason: A review that only confirms is biased.
units.rule: Include findings that contradict your assumptions, along with alternative interpretations.

units.reason: Readers can then judge how complete and fair the coverage is.
units.rule: Describe how you searched for and chose the literature, including the criteria for selection.

units.failure: needed context missing or unneeded sections added
units.reason: Not everything fits the main organising scheme, but extras must earn their place.
units.rule: Add short extra sections only where the reader needs them to place your study, such as the current situation, a history, or questions for further research.

units.failure: a sprawling review of an unbounded topic
units.reason: A tighter problem gives a sharper and more complete survey.
units.rule: Narrow the topic before you begin so that the number of sources to survey stays manageable.

units.failure: outdated sources or a missing history
units.reason: Expectations about how recent sources must be differ by field.
units.rule: Match the currency of sources to the discipline: some fields need the newest work, while a social science review may need to trace how views changed over time.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Learn how to write a review of literature

units.reason: Sources mean little until the reader knows what field of inquiry they belong to.
units.rule: Open by naming the topic or problem area so the reader has a setting for the sources that follow.

units.failure: list of sources with no overall picture
units.reason: This shows the reader the shape of the field before individual studies appear.
units.rule: Early on, describe the broad pattern in the published work: its trends, its disagreements over theory, method or evidence, or what remains unstudied.

units.failure: unexplained selection and ordering of sources
units.reason: Readers can only judge a review whose purpose, criteria and limits are declared.
units.rule: State your own angle on the literature, the standards you will use to compare sources, the order of the review, and where needed what is left out and why.

units.reason: Grouping turns a string of summaries into classification and comparison.
units.rule: Arrange sources into groups that share something, such as method, findings, aim or period, instead of treating them one after another.

units.failure: minor studies given equal space with major ones
units.reason: Readers infer significance from how long you dwell on a source.
units.rule: Give each study an amount of detail that matches its weight in the field; more words imply more importance.

units.reason: These aids let readers follow the comparisons and see why each one matters.
units.rule: Begin paragraphs with a sentence that covers the whole group, add guiding markers along the way, and insert short sentences that say what a comparison shows.

units.failure: conclusion that wanders from the opening focus
units.reason: The ending should resolve the review's stated purpose, not drift to new ground.
units.rule: Close by drawing together what the most important works have contributed, keeping to the focus the introduction set.

units.reason: Evaluation, not just summary, is what makes a review analytical and useful for planning research.
units.rule: Assess where knowledge now stands: name weaknesses of method, contradictions in theory or results, and questions that later studies should take up.

units.reason: The link shows why the body of work matters beyond its own narrow question.
units.rule: End by connecting the reviewed topic to a wider field, discipline or profession.

units.reason: Purpose and discipline change the format expected.
units.rule: Check what form the review must take, since it may stand alone or serve as the justification for new research in a proposal or thesis.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing an Abstract for Your Research Paper

units.failure: abstract that omits findings or significance
units.reason: A reader deciding whether to open the paper needs every major part of it represented in miniature.
units.rule: Cover, briefly, the background, the question, prior knowledge, the motive for the study, the methods, the main results and what they mean.

units.failure: abstract that depends on the paper to make sense
units.reason: Many readers use it alone to judge relevance and later to recall the main points.
units.rule: Write the abstract so that a person who never opens the full paper still understands what was studied and found.

units.reason: The abstract reports what this paper did, and the supporting literature belongs where it is discussed in full.
units.rule: Leave citations out of the abstract; describe your own study and argument, and keep references for the body of the paper.

units.reason: You cannot condense an argument accurately before you know what the finished paper says.
units.rule: Draft the abstract only after the full paper exists, even though it is printed first.

units.reason: Its job is a quick overview, and venues commonly impose their own length and format requirements.
units.rule: Keep the abstract to roughly one paragraph, in the region of 150 to 250 words, unless the journal or instructor sets another limit.

units.reason: Other researchers find the paper through searches that match on these words.
units.rule: Put the key terms of the study into the abstract and the title, because databases index papers from those two places.

units.reason: Tense signals to the reader whether a statement reports finished work or a claim that holds now.
units.rule: Choose tense by function: past for earlier studies and completed work, present for standing facts, for what the paper argues and for what the results imply.

units.reason: Fields weight background, method and results differently, and some journals fix the layout.
units.rule: Adjust how much space each element gets, and their order, to the discipline and the kind of paper; use labelled sections when the journal demands a structured form.

pages.by: a model in a QueryBook build session
pages.title: Writing Public Comments on Proposed Regulations

units.failure: an opinion-only comment that is discounted
units.reason: Agency staff weigh evidence above opinion, unlike elected officials who count what constituents think.
units.rule: Build a comment to a regulator on data and concrete real-world effects, not on how strongly you feel about the proposal.

units.failure: a comment with no stated standing
units.reason: The reviewer needs a ground for treating the writer as a relevant voice.
units.rule: Begin by saying who you are and which experience or vantage point makes your input worth the agency's attention.

units.failure: remarks that cannot be matched to a provision
units.reason: A reviewer must be able to attach each remark to one piece of the proposal.
units.rule: Name the regulation, sum it up briefly, and point to the exact portion your remarks address.

units.reason: A stance without support gives the agency nothing it can act on.
units.rule: Declare your position, then back it with sourced data and with the likely effects on you or on other people.

units.failure: repeating what the agency already knows
units.reason: Fresh information is where an outside writer has the best chance of changing the outcome.
units.rule: Give the most room to facts the regulator has probably not seen or considered yet.

units.failure: an abstract objection with no stakes
units.reason: The source reports that such consequences make a comment carry more weight.
units.rule: Connect your point to what the rule would do to people's costs or to their health.

units.reason: A hostile tone lowers the weight a reader gives to the substance.
units.rule: Stay respectful toward the subject even where you reject the premise behind the regulation.

units.reason: Reviewers outside your field must be able to follow the point.
units.rule: Use everyday wording and leave specialist jargon out of the comment.

units.reason: Identical wording suggests the sender has not thought the matter through independently.
units.rule: Write your own text; do not send a form letter that matches what other commenters submit.

units.reason: Unrelated matter weakens the force of the points that do matter.
units.rule: Leave out material that does not bear on the provision you are discussing.

units.reason: The source says clear organisation makes a comment easier to absorb and more effective.
units.rule: Give the comment an evident structure so a reviewer can take in each part quickly.
